items.title: Yankees news: Brian Cashman taps bullpen as top priority
items.author: Nick Power
items.content:
MLB.com | Bryan Hoch: After the conclusion of the annual GM meetings this week, the Yankees’ offseason priorities are beginning to come into focus. Brian Cashman acknowledged in an interview that rebuilding his bullpen tops the list. “Two of the three pitchers going into our eighth and ninth inning are gone; (Paul) Blackburn and (David) Bednar right now are free agents, so we’ve got our work to do,” the Yankees GM said. “And because of that, I am casting a wide net.”

Options include reunions with free agents Bednar, Blackburn, Tim Hill, and Jonathan Loáisiga as well as Adrian Morejon, who was linked to the Yankees while with the Padres this past season. Other potential areas for improvement include third base, second base, and catcher.

The Athletic | Chris Kirschner: ($) Speaking of third base, the Yankees were linked to Alec Bohm on Thursday by Ken Rosenthal and Will Sammon. Kirschner is skeptical that the former Phillie can be the solution, noting he was below average at the dish last year and has been the worst defender at the hot corner in all of baseball since debuting in 2020. While Bohm’s right-handed bat could provide some platoon advantages, Kirschner suggests the money required to sign him would be better allocated elsewhere — like making a play for Japanese phenom Teruaki Sato, Texas’ Corey Seager, or Houston’s Isaac Paredes.

FanGraphs | Matthew Roberson: After another disappointing October, an overarching look at where the Yankees go from here. Roberson recaps some of the problems at hand — an aging roster, thin farm system, and depleted coaching staff — before pinpointing what he believes to be the core issue. Since signing DJ LeMahieu before the 2019 season, the most impactful external free agent position player Cashman has brought in is Paul Goldschmidt, the aging future Hall of Famer who’s been a helpful part-time player but is no longer the type of impact bat the Yankees may need to get over the top. If Cashman eschews a major addition to the lineup this offseason, Roberson predicts one more year of World Series drought.

items.title: Pacers 106, Knicks 104: “I’m sure Indiana will look like an all star team tonight.”
items.author: Russell Richardson
items.content:
Daltong called it. “I’m sure Indiana will look like an all star team tonight.” The Hoosiers may have entered the game 4–8 overall and 1–4 at home, but even while weathering the absence of Tyrese Haliburton, they have another gear available to them. For instance, on Veterans Day, when they ripped open the fourth quarter with 14 unanswered points. Or tonight, when they outscored the Knicks (6–6) by 13 early in the final frame and held on for a 106–104 win.

Tonight’s tilt at Gainbridge Fieldhouse was another Group B game in the NBA Cup tourney. The Knicks were favored because they’re the more talented team on paper, but their effort showed up too late to steal the win. They were simply out-hustled for most of the game. In the positive column, Karl-Anthony Towns registered his twelfth straight double-double (23 PTS, 15 RBS), breaking Willis Reed’s franchise record for consecutive double-doubles to start a season. And Mikal Bridges took 12 shots! For 18 points! On the less positive side, Josh Hart went scoreless on four shots, the Knicks lost the paint by 20 and second-chance points by nine, and yet again they attempted double-digit fewer free throws than their opponent (IND 18-of-25, NYK 10-of-13).

Shield your eyes from all this yellow . . . looks a little like a filthy urinal.

The game started inelegantly, with Andrew Nembhard (12 PTS, 4-14 FG, 6 AST, 6 TO) taking the opening tip in for an easy layup. At the other end, Hart thought KAT was going to cut. Instead, KAT crowded Jalen Brunson (33 PTS, 11-22 FG, 11 AST, +8) along the arc, and Nembhard deflected Hart’s pass out of bounds. That kind of confusion is predictable this early in the season, especially with Hart having missed a few games already. So is KAT’s ability to steamroll Ivica Zubac (12 PTS, 13 RBS) for snacks at the cup.

OG Anunoby (11 PTS, 4-13 FG, +8) laced an early triple when Hart noticed that Pascal Siakam (19 PTS, 5-13 FG) was napping in transition. OG and Pascal have a history, and they made each other’s jobs difficult for most of the night. (After that three, OG would make one of his next seven attempts.)

The Knicks took control with a 9–0 run that turned a 9–9 tie into an 18–9 lead. Towns scored seven of those nine and finished the quarter with 12 points and three rebounds. The oft-maligned Bridges chipped in six points and a steal (welcome back!), and Hart had four boards and three dimes. Brunson scored just two points but set up three baskets before picking up his second foul, an offensive foul, and heading to the bench.

Jay Huff brought Indiana back with eight quick points off the bench, including two threes and an alley-oop from that pest T.J. McConnell. Miles McBride answered with a longball, but the Knicks went more than three minutes without scoring after that. Deuce missed his next three attempts, Shamet bricked a couple, and Huff blocked Andre Drummond at the rim. Indiana went on a 15–5 run, taking a 24–23 lead on an OAKAAKUYOAK Obi Toppin bank shot. Towns returned and restored the lead with a driving and-one. The good guys were up 27–26 at the horn.

If you enjoyed the stanky shooting and one-and-dones of the first quarter, the Knicks cordially invited you to more of the same in the second. OG tied it at 31 on another Towns-as-hub laser, then Indy rattled off a 13–4 run. Toppin laced a three and finished a fast break, while Zubac elbowed his way to three O-boards on one possession before putting it in. No Diawara tonight, but Pacôme Dadiet made a brief (as in one minute) appearance in the second.

Yet again, free throws were the biggest bugaboo. In their last game, the Knicks shot 14 fewer free throws than Cleveland. In tonight’s second quarter, Indiana went 13-of-17 while New York shot . . . 1-of-2. Call the vet! These zebras have rabies!

Brunson scored half of the team’s 22 second-quarter points. Towns grabbed six rebounds but scored just two points, and Josh Hart, Landry Shamet, and Miles McBride all fired blanks. Aaron Nesmith scored six straight, the last on a technical free throw after Mike Brown drew a tech, to stretch Indiana’s lead to 14. Brunson hit a turnaround and fed Tyler Kolek for a late three to regain some ground. Indy led 58–49 at the break.

Through the first half, our heroes were dishing the ball fine, with seven more assists than the Hoosiers. Rebounds and points in the paint were basically a dead heat. The voodoo was in the fouls. The Knicks had committed twice as many as the Pacers (14–7). And somehow Rick Carlisle found it necessary to complain about the calls.

On to the third. Cap was cooking, with 16 points and four dimes. The Knicks needed it all and then some. Brunson led an 8–0 run that brought New York within five, but the comeback stalled before they could get back to black. Kelly Oubre Jr. and Nesmith each scored seven in the period, Zubac added six points and five boards, and the hosts were up by 14 again.

From there, the Knicks closed on a 15–2 run to get within a point. McBride hit two bombs, Shamet added one, and Drummond grabbed three defensive boards and a steal. Deuce and Anunoby both missed chances to take the lead in the final eight seconds, so the Knicks went into the fourth trailing 85–84.

From there, two scenarios were possible. Either the Champs would maintain their momentum and turn back those pesky Pacers, or Indy would do what they did against the Wiz on Wednesday and go on some crazy run. ’Twas the latter, fans. After Anunoby tied it at 87, the hosts answered with a 15–2 run. Nembhard scored six points in the quarter, Oubre added five points and two steals, and Zubac finished with nine offensive boards. The Knicks kept fumbling and bumbling the ball away. This time Captain Clutch couldn’t save them either, managing only four points in the fourth after scoring 16 in the third.

Behold the bumbling and fumbling of which I wrote:

New York still had a shot to tie it in the final minute. Brunson’s layup with 26 seconds left cut the deficit to four, and after Siakam missed both free throws, Bridges (!) hit a pull-up to make it 106–104. Anunoby picked off Siakam’s pass with three seconds left, but Towns missed a 15-foot turnaround and the Pacers held on. Ballgame.

If you’re feeling testy after another loss, so is Jose Alvarado. Evidently, he and Quenton Jackson have prior history of physical scrapes (including an altercation when Alvarado was still with the Pelicans). Jackson not only taunted Jalen Brunson tonight, but in the third quarter he jawed at Rick Brunson, too. Jose might be out of the rotation, but the big dawg is always ready to defend his captain!

Up to Toronto our heroes go to play the Raps on Sunday. This is your recap, chaps. Safe travels, Knickerbockers.

items.title: 'I'm happy I'm still alive and able to continue to try to live my dream of a WorldTour career' – Ex-Ineos talent Theodor Storm signs for new team after nightmare three years
items.author: Patrick Fletcher
items.content:
When Theodor Storm signed for the Ineos team at the age of 18, on a three-year contract starting in 2024, it looked like we had another teenaged super-talent, jumping straight from the juniors to set the WorldTour alight. Three years on, it’s fair to say things have not gone to plan, though it’s unfair to say any of that is Storm’s fault.

On Friday, it was announced that Storm was signing for the Danish third-division team, ColoQuick, in a bid to revive a career that has seen two huge setbacks.

Storm’s debut season with Ineos in 2024 was wiped out entirely after he was diagnosed with the rare auto-immune disease, Guillain-Barré syndrome, at the start of the year, which left him in intensive care for two weeks, a rehabilitation centre for two months, and unfit for the best part of two years.

However, as in 2024, he had not raced at all this year, mainly due to breaking bones in his back at a track training camp towards the end of 2025.

“Shit happens, but I'm happy that I'm still alive and able to continue to try to live my dream of a WorldTour career,” Storm said in a transfer announcement from ColoQuick on Friday.

“Now I'm ready to give it a good shot again, and I'm glad that ColoQuick is giving me the opportunity. ColoQuick is the right place for me. It's a strong team with a great program and an almost professional set-up.”

As for his troubles with Guillain-Barré syndrome, he added: “It went well in comparison to the doctors' assessment, but we must acknowledge that it has taken at least two years in cycle.”

'Theodor's talent is still there'

ColoQuick revealed that Storm had in fact signed a contract with the team for the 2024 season, but just three days later received an offer from Ineos, and they let him take it.

Having never raced in an Ineos jersey – 2024 and 2026 were write-offs and 2025 was with the affiliated team – Storm was in some ways picking up where he left off three years ago.

“We’re really looking forward to starting again. He never managed to pull in our jersey in 2024 but in return we get a rider back with a lot in the luggage, who has to find his way back to the professional world,” said the team’s Sports Manager Christian Moberg.

“Theodor's talent is still there, but the many setbacks have costed both physically and mentally, we need to control them before we start setting big goals."

items.title: The surprising convergence behind F1's increasingly competitive 2026 season
Lighter, stiffer, but is it more aero? We wind tunnel tested the Giant Propel
items.author: andy@atpperformance.uk (Andy Turner)
items.content:
The Giant Propel was updated for 2026, although you'd be hard-pressed to tell it apart from the outgoing model, and in doing so, it achieved the bifecta of bike launch goals, cutting both weight and aero drag numbers; the latter by a significant claimed amount.

A full build comes in at a claimed 6.56kg in a size medium, meaning you'll need to bolt on some extra weight somewhere to meet the 6.8kg UCI limit. The biggest headline figures for this bike versus the previous one, though, were a full system aero approach which contributed to an overall 18.4 watt saving.

Not all of that came in aerodynamic terms, with some attributed to tyre rolling resistance too, but it saw aero gains from the frame, the new Cadex Max 50 wheels and the new aero tyres.

The biggest relative gain, though, is the new narrower handlebar. Given that a rider makes up most of the drag, the new bars with 40cm drops and 37cm hoods are designed to allow for a more aerodynamic rider position.

Our protocol has remained consistent since our first wind tunnel test, so that we can reliably compare as many bikes as possible, even when testing across different days and years.

You can find in-depth details on how the testing was conducted in our 2025 aero bike shootout article, but to refresh memories, I'll outline what we did here.

As with all our other tests, we start by testing the bike as it comes from the factory. The only caveat here is that we use the same front tyre, as that has a significant impact on total aerodynamic performance, especially when just testing the frame and wheels.

Wheels, groupset, and finishing kit remain the same, but we set the bikes up to have consistent saddle heights and handlebar positions.

This gives us an interesting insight into how the bike performs in isolation. Although not relevant to real-world riding, it allows us to compare the bikes with a smaller error margin.

Of course, bikes don't ride themselves, so we always test with a rider present as well.

Our rider and position are kept consistent, while the wind tunnel takes 'edge' files so we can match the rider position for every run and across different days.

Rider-on testing always has a larger margin of error, and we test for 30 seconds per run rather than 10 seconds per run so we can smooth out the data and quieten down the data 'noise'.

A pedalling mannequin would be the gold standard way to combine those tests, and while it's on the roadmap for , it wasn't available in time for this test. Notably, Giant has its own pedalling mannequin, called Grischa. This is based on a scan of former pro Grischa Niermann, who nowadays works as Sports Director at Lidl-Trek.

Its latest version, Grischa 2.0, can adapt to different positions for gravel bike testing too (we have a test of the Giant Revolt coming soon), and this was used to develop and validate the Propel's claimed improvements.

  1. Bike only, control wheels

Given that some frames come with wheels specifically designed to work best with those frames - think Roval and Specialized, Reserve and Cervélo, Cadex with Giant - we also test with a control set of wheels.

We use a set of ENVE SES 4.5 wheels with 28mm Continental GP5000 S TR tyres. This also allows us to narrow down where performance comes from. A bike that comes with a 60mm front wheel might outperform a frame that comes with a 40mm wheel. Adding a control wheel test lets us see if those performance differences are down to just the frame, the wheels, or a combination of the two.

We have also done separate tests on wheels, so for the Look 795 Blade RS (2026) that came with the super-fast Scope Artech 6 wheels, we can see that adding the ENVEs dropped the relative performance. Likewise, the ENVE Melee V2 with ENVE 6.7 Pro wheels gave us an idea of where those wheels might sit in the overall table based on their comparative result against the 4.5 model.

We tested across yaw angles (the angle the wind hits the bike) of -15°, -10°, -5°, 0°, 5°, 10° and 15° to allow us to assess crosswind performance. For reference, Giant's in-house testing goes out to 20°, which its engineers believe offers a fairer reflection of real-world experience.

Testing itself is conducted at 40km/h, chosen as a speed that the majority of buyers may expect to go on their faster-paced group rides, group events, or giving a road bike time trial a go. Most bikes are advertised at 45-50kph, in part because of the speed of pro races, but also because larger differences in watt savings tend to appear the higher the speed. We set 40kph as a more realistic benchmark, and we appreciate everyone will go faster than this at points, but that'll mostly be with the support of a tailwind or a hill.

To try and standardise things, we ensure all testing is done in the same gear, so rear mech placement is similar, and with the same front tyres, as they are the first thing the wind impacts. Position on the bike is kept as close as possible, and kit, helmet, glasses, and shoes are consistent from test to test.

Two Elite Vico cages with Elite Fly bottles are fitted to each bike, save for when the bike comes with aero bottle cages as standard, such as the Colnago Y1RS or Factor ONE. This is because those are included parts of a bike, and people are unlikely to remove them (in favour of something nominally worse), so we feel it's fair to test them as part of the entire system.

To have a baseline, we have our Trek Emonda ALR control bike, which is now a full-time wind tunnel test bike. We test at the start and end of each day to ensure atmospheric conditions have remained consistent, while we also make sure that results correlate with prior test visits.

And as ever, the caveat applies that our tests aren't the be-all and end-all of a bike's performance. Aerodynamics is just one part of a bike's overall design, and Giant itself says that for the Propel, it "developed and tested the frame, cockpit, wheels and tyres together as one complete system, balancing aero performance with rolling resistance, weight, efficiency, compliance and handling."

What's more, other testers may get different results under different wind tunnel or aero-testing protocols. Our data is subject to an error margin, the size of which is outlined within the results.

In our data, the new Propel Advanced SL 0 is 3.45w faster than the previous model.

Interestingly, performance at higher yaw was where it struggled relatively more. Perhaps the shorter tube profiles impacted the performance here, as the sail effect is more limited than with deeper-profile tubes.

You can see here that the bike now sits at the top of the bottom third out of all the bikes we tested, 7.45w away from the Factor ONE.

However, to be fair to Giant, part of the improved performance versus the previous model is the aero tyres, which we removed from the front in order to avoid skewed results. Likewise, the narrower bars, which have minimal impact on performance when the rider is not present.

When we put a rider on the bike, it's a relatively similar picture. Again, I will caveat here, as with the Merida Reacto One 2026, we had set a testing protocol for the drops in a consistent position, rather than narrow or flared hoods.

Both the Giant and Merida rely on the narrower tops to allow for a narrower, classic breakaway style of riding.

We can see here that with a rider on, the gap actually broadens to the top of the field, now 8.21w slower than the Cervelo S5, and with the rider on producing generally smaller wattage gaps, the percentage difference between the Cervelo and the Giant is actually larger.

This also sends the Giant down the field further and only 0.47w faster than the previous model. Our margin of error, of course, means it could be up into the top 10, but it could also drop it to the slowest of the bunch.

When we add the control wheels, things do not get better for the Propel's overall picture, but it does at least show that the new Cadex Max 50 wheels are faster on this frame than the ENVE SES 4.5 wheels are, as switching wheels resulted in one of the larger swings in performance, with a 2.55w decrease in performance compared to the standard Cadex wheels.

Overall, then, a surprising set of results for the new Giant Propel Advanced SL 0, seeing it very close to the previous generation, and struggling to move up the table while others like the Look and ENVE have made great strides with the latest releases from those brands.

It's a difficult one to unpack here. The Propel tested previously and the new 2026 model look nearly identical, save for a greater drop in the seatstays. Most of the specific frame differences are reductions in weight and also rideability improvements, which we will cover in a full review.

Our testing protocol admittedly does impact Giant negatively, given that several of the key aero improvements were elements that we had to switch out for the sake of test controls. The Cadex aero tyre was gone, although Giant's 0.42w saving is not massive, and we tested our rider-on tests in the drops, not the tops. This is a similar predicament to the Merida Reacto, which builds on most of the aero savings from getting the rider into a narrower position. But then really we're testing rider position, not the bike in some isolation.

Saying that, ENVE have a similar design with the SES Pro bars, as they have long used narrow tops and flared drops to balance aero and stability. But with the Melee V2, testing in the drops did not handicap the bike, even with the aero drop shape and bar tape designed to minimise the drag produced by the drops with a rider in the tops.

What we can say for the new Propel is that the Cadex Max 50 wheels are now faster, but given the minimal differences to the frame, aero performance is near unchanged. It is lighter, though, and with the 14.8% increase in ‘system handling efficiency’, we trust it will ride even better, although we will determine that in full testing.

items.title: Tearful Pochettino says United job was ‘difficult to turn down’ in USMNT farewell
items.author: Pablo Iglesias Maurer in Fayetteville, Georgia
items.content:
• Coach was ‘transparent’ in dealings with club, federation

  • Pochettino had signed deal to stay with US through 2030

There were always going to be tears at Mauricio Pochettino’s news conference at US Soccer’s national training center on Friday. It was only a matter of when. Pochettino is famously emotional, and nobody in attendance had to wait long for the waterworks – they came during his introductory remarks, as he thanked the US Soccer executives flanking him for the opportunity to guide the US men. He grew emotional again as he addressed his impending departure for Manchester United, one announced just hours earlier.

“I think [the decision was],” Pochettino said, pausing to compose himself, “one of the most difficult decisions of our careers. Thank you guys. Thank you so much.”

items.title: Yankees Birthday of the Day: Mel Stottlemyre
items.author: Matt Ferenchick
items.content:
Mel Stottlemyre had the misfortune of being one of the best Yankees’ players during one of the worst periods in Yankees’ history. Through no fault of Stottlemyre’s own, the Yankees slide down the standings during his tenure, mostly as a result of the disastrous CBS ownership period. He has the status of being on the shortlist of best ever Yankees’ players who never won a World Series.

However, Stottlemyre then had a coaching career that more than made up for it. He later became the pitching coach on the Yankees’ 1900s and 2000s dynasty, arguably getting more fame for that than his playing career. However, he was great at both and on this — what would’ve been his 85th birthday — let’s remember a legendary Yankee.

Melvin Leon “Mel” Stottlemyre November 13, 1941 (Hazleton, MO) January 13, 2019 (Seattle, WA) 1964-74

One of five children born to Vernon and Lorene Ellen Stottlemyre, Mel Stottlemyre was born in Missouri 1941. His father was a pipefitter and moved the family around to various states around the country before they finally settled in Washington state. There, Mel developed a love of baseball from his father, who would take him and his brother to local semi-pro games.

Early in his life, Stottlemyre’s playing of the sport was mostly limited to games in the backyard with his brother. He didn’t really play much organized ball until high school. Stottlemyre began to shine as a pitcher and shortstop for Mabton High School, where he was a multi-sport start and the student body president.

His high school career got Stottlemyre a scholarship to Yakima Valley Junior College, but things did not start great there. His first season was supposed to be in 1960, but poor grades led him to be declared academically ineligible. He eventually got that straightened out and returned for 1961, where he impressed and caught the eye of major league teams.

The then Milwaukee Braves gave Stottlemyre a workout, but came away unimpressed and rejected him for “not throwing hard enough.” Their loss would be the Yankees’ gain. Yankees scout Eddie Taylor signed Stottlemyre to the pitcher’s childhood favorite team in 1961.

After making quick work of the lower levels of the minors, Stottlemyre struggled in Triple-A in 1963. Having previously been one of the hottest prospects in the Yankees’ system, that led to him not getting an invite to big league spring training for 1964. However, after starting the season in the Triple-A bullpen, he battled his way back into the rotation and put in a monster season. By the end of the year, with Whitey Ford dealing with injury issues, Stottlemyre got a big league callup. Making his debut in August, Stottlemyre appeared in 13 games in 1964, putting up a 2.04 ERA in 96 innings. He helped rejuvenate that Yankee team, allowing them to eke out the AL pennant.

In that year’s World Series, manager Yogi Berra entrusted the rookie to make three World Series starts. Stottlemyre outdueled Bob Gibson in a Game 2 victory. Gibson and the Cardinals would get the better of Stottlemyre and the Yankees in the other two — including Game 7 — but there’s no way to not be impressed by what the 22-year-old had done that year.

Unfortunately, those would be the only postseason games Stottlemyre ever pitched in, through no fault of his own. Over the course of his 11-year career, Stottlemyre put up a 2.97 ERA, a 3.36 FIP, 40.7 rWAR, and 34.0 fWAR. He was named an All-Star on five occasions and won 20 games on three occasions. However, he also finished with double digit losses on eight occasions, as the pieces of the 1950s/early ‘60s dynasty aged out and a lot of the young non-Stottlemyre players couldn’t hold up their end of the bargain.

Eventually, the years of being one of the team’s few hopes and throwing 250+ innings caught up to Stottlemyre. Just as the team was beginning to turn the corner under a new crop of youngsters and was getting purchased by George Steinbrenner, Stottlemyre tore his rotator cuff. While he attempted to make a comeback, the team eventually released him in March 1975. He decided to end his playing career, just barely missing out on some great year in franchise history at either end of his years in New York.

Having moved back to Washington, Stottlemyre got into coaching with the Mariners in the early 1980s. The Mets eventually brought him back to New York as their pitching coach in 1984. Mentoring the likes of a young Dwight Gooden, Stottlemyre helped the Mets to their famous 1986 World Series championship. After that, he spent some years with the Astros before Joe Torre brought him back into the fold after being hired as Yankees’ manager in 1996.

Over the next many years, Stottlemyre finally got to be part of postseason success in the Bronx. As the Yankees’ pitching guru, he helped them to World Series championships in 1996, ‘98, ‘99, and 2000. He eventually retired after the 2005 season, in part likely due to frustrations over George Steinbrenner’s George Steinbrenner-ness. After a stint in the Diamondbacks’ organization, he returned to the dugout for one season as Mariners’ pitching coach in 2008 before retiring again.

Stottlemyre had two sons also make the big leagues as pitchers in Mel Jr. and Todd. Todd had a very solid 14-year career, winning the World Series with the 1992 and ‘93 Blue Jays. Mel Jr. only briefly played in the majors, but he followed his dad into the pitching coach field. He was mostly recently the Marlins’ pitching coach, departing that role after the 2024 season.

Mel himself returned to the pacific northwest after his baseball career was over. Having previously beaten the disease, Stottlemyre eventually passed away from cancer in 2019 at age 77. Thankfully before that, he got to return to Yankee Stadium on occasions. That included a 2015 appearance, where he gave an emotional speech after the team surprised him with a Monument Park plaque.

Mel Stottlemyre held two roles in his years with the Yankees and was great at both of them. He probably would’ve been great at other ones too.

See more of the “Yankees Birthday of the Day” series here.

items.title: Why aerodynamics will become "even more important" under 2027 MotoGP regulations
Exquisite titanium, AI-enabled concept bikes, 32-inch gravel tech and even a new rim brake bike: All the tech that caught our eye at Rouleur Live 2026
items.author: william.jones@futurenet.com (Will Jones)
items.content:
As another summer fades into distant memory, and thermal bib tights become the norm, the annual Rouleur Live show has rolled around once again.

This year, with Mathieu Van der Poel roped in for an interview on stage with his friend and fellow Canyon athlete Freddy Ovett, the weekend kicked off with the duo joining Rosa Kloser and hundreds of fans for laps around Regent's Park.

As ever, the show attracted some big names, with Kasia Niewiadoma-Phinney and Taylor Phinney taking to the stage, as well as Bradley and Ben Wiggins.

But our attention was elsewhere. Our focus lay on the halls packed with bikes, tech and more.

Despite being the last trade show of the year and one that typically focuses on pro or custom tech more so than new releases, there were a few never-before-seen things for us to feast our eyes on this year too.

That includes the new Van Rysel RCR-R Pro, a first look at an all-new Winspace, a Kask helmet, and, as has been the big trend of 2026, a smattering of new 32" wheeled gravel bikes.

Get yourself a cup of tea and settle in for all the pictures from the wanderings of Cyclingnews' tech extraordinaire, Will Jones.

items.title: Presenting the 2026 Yankees Roster Report Cards
items.author: Pinstripe Alley Staff
items.content:
Now that we are steadily moving into the offseason with the 2026 Yankees’ disappointing ALDS loss to the Rays thankfully growing more distant to the present day, it’s time for Pinstripe Alley’s very own Roster Report Card series, where our staff evaluates and assigns grades to the most relevant players on the roster.

This series is scheduled to begin in mid-October and run through early December, skipping only Thanksgiving and weekends. We’ll start with the free agents who are imminently likely to hit the market and then proceed alphabetically. Missing from this series are Yankees manager Aaron Boone and general manager Brian Cashman, but you can find their evaluations by visiting the highlighted links.

As a reminder, the writer for a specific player isn’t assigning their own grade; these grades are averaged from our entire staff’s submissions.

items.title: Yankees 2026 Roster Report Cards: Luis García Jr.
items.author: Joshua Diemert
items.content:
It’s very tempting to want to love Luis García Jr. His lefty swing reminds me so much of Robinson Canó, and indeed my own swing is modeled after the former Yankee All-Star. At the time the Yankees dealt for him, desperate to get some kind of thump in an Aaron Judge-less lineup, he led the National League in slugging. When he came to New York, he clubbed a long home run in his second game, a worthy introduction to the Bronx faithful. After that, he was fine in the regular season, dreadful in October, and now is the source of a bit of a logjam on the roster.

2026 Stats (With Yankees): 43 G, 169 PA, 21 R, 42 H, 6 2B, 7 HR, 16 RBI, 1 SB, .264/.302/.434, 102 OPS+, 104 wRC+, 0.5 fWAR, 0.6 bWAR.

Arb eligible

To Brian Cashman’s credit he made more than one deal for bats at the deadline, but neither Heliot Ramos nor García Jr. really had the impact I’m sure he planned. Luis came in in grand style:

Will forever love you, Ruocco.

That the Yankees went on to lose that game, one of the stupider of the year and what a list that makes, maybe says something about García Jr. as a Yankee. Getting him was the right move, it just never really paid off. I was surprised to see that he actually managed an 87 wRC+ in the postseason, because I genuinely would have thought he posted half of that.

To be fair, he was On One against the Red Sox in the Wild Card Series, hitting .500, but then kind of everyone did that against the Red Sox in those two games. Facing the Rays in the ALDS Luis went 1-for-10, a -56 wRC+. The Yankees only who played three games against the Rays, if García Jr. went 1-for-10 in a random series in July we probably wouldn’t even notice, but it happened when the lights were brightest.

I’ve said this a lot about the 2026 Yankees, but Luis didn’t really do himself many favors. Yes, he has that big home run in his second game against the Cardinals, then he went two weeks without another dinger. He slugged .560 in Washington, .434 in New York. His strikeout rate jumped five points.

I do wonder how much the dimensions of Yankee Stadium worked against him. Luis was on pace for 33 doubles across 600 PA while with the Nationals, down to 22 over 600 PA in the Bronx. Yankee Stadium is a tremendous ballpark to hit home runs in, and not very friendly to other kinds of extra-base hits. The short right field wall was absolutely a reason why the club brought Heliot Ramos in, and maybe they believed that smooth lefty swing would turn some of those doubles into dingers for García Jr., but that didn’t happen, at least in 2026.

Moving into 2027, the Yankee have once again assembled a roster with so many first base/DH types. Giancarlo Stanton will be on the roster, Ben Rice is not going to be a catcher, Aaron Judge will almost certainly see less time in the outfield than we’re used to, if for no other reason than the game’s best hitter needs to sometimes be saved from himself. Then there’s García Jr., who on paper is possibly a better hitter than Stanton but not better than Rice or Judge, but also probably isn’t good enough at second base to merit uprooting Anthony Volpe.

Maybe that’s the project for this winter, making Luis García Jr. a functional second baseman and stick him in some kind of first base/second base platoon role. This gets complicated if there’s a lockout and teams can’t communicate with players, and is further complicated by the fact that the very bad Washington Nationals gave Luis 0 innings at the keystone last year.

I want to love Luis García Jr. I don’t think his performance in 2026 merits that love. I am hopeful, perhaps foolishly, that it will in 2027.

items.title: 'I was getting less and less enjoyment from modern cycling' – Julian Alaphilippe opens up for first time about retirement and knowing when to stop
items.author: Matilda Price
items.content:
French starl Julian Alaphilippe has spoken publicly for the first time since his retirement, saying that he was losing enjoyment in cycling and is happy to be out of the limelight.

Since retirement, the Frenchman has laid relatively low, but was the guest of honour at a French Cycling Federation (FFC) event on Thursday evening and spoke about his decision to end his career as he addressed the audience in a speech.

Speaking with emotion in his voice, according to , Alaphilippe said he was "even happier with his decision" after watching a montage of his best moments and thanking the FFC for a "touching" tribute.

"I always wanted to stop at the right time, not to do one year too many," he said. "I was getting less and less enjoyment from modern cycling.

"I still felt useful to my team, but I felt it was time to turn the page. I am very happy to have accomplished everything I have done over the years."

'Now I need a bit of shade'

His accomplishments include two world titles, six Tour de France stage victories including a long stint in the yellow jersey in 2019, and victories at Milan-San Remo, Strade Bianche and La Flèche Wallonne. He has also represented France at the Olympic Games.

He ended his career widely considered as one of the best French cyclists of the last two decades, but it was stepping away from that celebration and adoration that was part of his motivation to retire.

"I've had enough of the limelight during my career and now I need a bit of shade," Alaphilippe said.

“Cycling was my outlet, but I’m happy to have stopped. I have a lot of gratitude. I was lucky enough to spend a decade and a half cycling, where I enjoyed myself, where it was my outlet, and where I gave emotions to my family, to people, to kids, to myself. I pushed myself to the limit to achieve the goals I set for myself."

He also gave special thanks to two important figures in his life, fellow pro and now French national coach Thomas Voeckler, as well as his cousin and long-term coach Franck Alaphilippe.

Despite briefly returning to the spotlight on Thursday evening, there is still no indication of what Alaphilippe may do next, and if he has a future in cycling, in 2027 or beyond.

Outside of cycling, he has a five-year-old son with his partner Marion Rousse, former pro and the director of the Tour de France Femmes.

items.title: 'It's looking very promising' – Remco Evenepoel delivers first reaction to favourable Tour de France 2027 route
items.author: Patrick Fletcher
items.content:
The time trial World Champion was the best of the rest behind Tadej Pogačar at this year’s Tour de France, and has been handed a favourable route next summer, with some 71 kilometres against the clock – the most since 2012.

On top of that, there are relatively few big mountain stages, with only two true summit finishes, as the organisers look to maintain suspense until the final week and the potentially decisive queen stage on stage 18.

"Pretty happy, obviously," Evenepoel said on the podcast of his bike sponsor, Specialized, recorded a couple of weeks ago and released on Thursday.

"I think it’s already a big step forward compared to last year’s, when we had a 26k individual time trial and a 20k team time trial. The year before was even less. So it’s great.

"I mean, a 38k and a 33k TT… The first one, from what I’ve seen is not technical at all, with long straights, so that’s really something that should suit me. Then the one in Toulouse is pretty flat until the little climb, I think it’s like a three-minute climb, so that’s something that suits me as well.

"I’m very happy," he added. "If you see it’s the most amount of time trial since 2012… still if you compare it to 2012 it’s quite a bit less, but I’m happy. It’s good. I would love it to be even a bit longer, but I’m very happy with what we got.

"Overall it’s looking very promising, the Tour," Evenepoel concluded.

With a stage win on the Plateau de Solaison this year and no slip-ups in the final week, Evenepoel proved that climbing is hardly a weakness, though compared to his time trialling it’s less of a weapon, and he has been prone to off-days, even this season.

"Probably this year was suiting me even less than in 2024 but still I got second. I knew somewhere I was able to do it but having that much climbing in the last days was something new for me to show to myself and the cycling world," he said.

"But it’s true that with those time trials and the more punchy finishes towards the beginning, and with – what is it? – three summit finishes, it’s something that’s fitting me better than having 10 summit finishes."

Evenepoel, in a surefire sign that he’s building his season around the Tour de France once again, said he has already been thinking about how the race might play out for him next July.

And within the context of the race itself, he's building his race around those two time trials, the first covering 38km from Blois to Chambord on stage 7, the second kicking off the final week on stage 16 with 33km in Toulouse.

"We need to make kind of a race strategy to arrive to those at those TTs as fresh as possible and really drop the hammer big time. It’s a nice opportunity to take two stage wins and next to that obviously comes the time gaps for GC," he said.

"The run-in towards first TT is not crazy hard – there are some tricky stages but no big mountains. Then from the first TT there are two or three really tough days. It shows that I can take nice little advantage before going into the Alps, which will help. It can also give some comfort in the mind, going into the Alps with an advantage."

items.title: Was Madrid F1 race an economic upgrade on Barcelona?
items.author: Samarth Kanal
items.content:
The inaugural 2026 Spanish Formula 1 Grand Prix at the Madring created €544 million in economic activity, supported 10,948 jobs, and generated €95m in tax revenue, according to its organiser.

The Madring is a part-street circuit built around the IFEMA conference centre - with the track layout set to be changed for 2027 to improve the quality of racing and frequency of overtaking.

The grand prix promoter ran a study conducted by PwC showing that, for every €1 of economic activity directly linked to the event, €4.60 was generated across Madrid’s wider economy.

The total economic impact was 16.5% larger than expected, the grand prix supported 23.7% more jobs than anticipated, and the overall tax contribution was 14.5% more than predicted.

In comparison to Madrid’s figure of €544m in economic activity for 2026, the Barcelona GP generated over €300m in local economic activity in 2024, according to its own reports. This was reaffirmed by Barcelona circuit CEO Pol Gilbert as part of the track’s recent extension announcement, where he said that “Formula 1 generates an economic impact of more than €300 million per edition” at the venue.

F1 CEO Stefano Domenicali recently said the US GP at Austin generated “over $1 billion” for the local area in 2026, while the Las Vegas GP has generated over $3.2bn cumulatively for the local area over its three editions.

IFEMA Madrid chairman Jose Vicente de los Mozos said that the figures “confirm the strategic importance the Grand Prix has gained for Madrid’s economy and international profile from its very first edition, generating economic activity equivalent to 0.16% of the Madrid Region’s GDP and 0.30% of the city of Madrid’s GDP”.

The grand prix attracted 353,000 attendees. The survey estimates that 35% of visitors were from overseas and 20% travelling from elsewhere in Spain - meaning 45% were from Madrid and its immediate vicinity.

International visitors spent an average of €2,772 per person over the course of their stay - compared with €1,099 from Spanish visitors and €659 among Madrid residents - with those figures including the estimated average ticket price, which is not stated.

International visitors to the grand prix therefore spent 1.7 times that of an average international tourist to Madrid, and 2.9 times more than an international tourist visiting Spain. Domestic visitors spent 3.8 times more than a domestic tourist would on a trip to the Madrid region.

Local digital publication Democrata found that hotel prices averaged €485 - 70% more than usual - for the grand prix.

Around 49% of visitors stayed in hotels, 32% in short-term rental accommodation, and 19% with family and friends - generating €95m in tax revenues.

Short-term rentals have been a contentious issue for the local area in recent years as, in 2025, the Spanish government cracked down on Airbnbs, removing nearly 66,000 listings across the country and fining the company €64m for illegal listings.

Furthermore, residents local to the Madring protested its environmental and societal impact, including noise concerns.

The survey found that 95.3% of international attendees said the grand prix had ‘enhanced Madrid’s international image’ and 98.1% would recommend Madrid as a tourist destination, with 86% of attendees saying they were likely to return.

PwC partner Jordi Esteve said: “Through extensive fieldwork, we have found that grand prix visitors spend more and stay longer than the average visitor. This is helping Madrid attract high-value tourism, generating greater economic activity and supporting employment.”

PwC conducted 1,102 face-to-face surveys between the Friday and Sunday of the race weekend.

items.title: 'The gap between second and first is humongous, and I've crossed that now' – Cameron Mason reflects on his breakthrough victory and that next piece of the puzzle
items.author: Patrick Fletcher
items.content:
On Wednesday, Cameron Mason found what he'd been looking for over a number of years: victory in a major international cyclo-cross race. Raising his arms in Niel, the 26-year-old Scot became the first British rider since Tom Pidcock in 2022 to win a round of the Superprestige series.

Mason has racked up plenty of top-fives since graduating from the U23s to the elites in 2022-2023, along with the odd podium, but in the biggest series like the World Cup or Superprestige, victory has eluded him. Until now.

In muddy conditions that suited his technical prowess, the 777tv CX Team rider got rid of Michael Vanthourenhout and Joran Wyseure on the final lap to solo to a victory that will go down as a breakthrough moment.

But where does he go from here? And what doors might this victory now open?

caught up with Mason the day after the race to hear about his sense of relief and satisfaction, how he channeled his frustrations from the European Championships, and how he's trying to be a more complete rider than ever this season.

CN: You said after the race in Niel that it maybe hadn't sunk in yet. With a night to sleep on it, has it done so?

Yeah, when I spoke after the race, I had spent the last hour kind of just doing it. Since Euros, I was just wanting to do the ride I knew I could do, or knew I could have done on Sunday. Then there wasn't much more to say because I felt like I'd just shown exactly what I wanted to do. So that was a nice feeling of 'no excuses', and I didn't need to dress anything up. It was just exactly what you saw, which was an hour of being in control and being strong enough and smart enough to be first across the line.

And it still feels pretty fresh. I haven't really got a plan for what's next, which is fine. So I'm just enjoying it for what it is now. But there wasn't much of a big celebration because there's also that little bit of like... it's annoying that it was coming for so long. It wasn't a surprise, basically. There wasn't that shock or anything. It was more like 'finally', and like 'there you go' – showing everyone that's what I thought I could do years ago, and I've done it now. So that was a very satisfying feeling.

CN: Is there a bit of relief in there as well, or a sort of pressure lifted?

Yeah, there's a bit of relief. I think. I mean, I could have spent the next five years chasing that, and that would have been fine. Every year, I really enjoy the puzzle, and putting all the puzzle pieces together in pursuit of that next thing. The next thing happened to be winning a bike race, but three years ago, the next thing was getting on the podium, and before that, it was getting a professional contract. The goalposts just moved and so now, clearly the next thing is to win again, but that feels less daunting than it did.

The gap between getting second and first is humongous, it’s vast. Mentally and physically, the difference between being second best and being best is huge, and I've crossed that now. I'm not sure what I've learned yet, but I think when I turn up at the start line the next few races, I'll realise, 'OK, that's that's what changed'.

If I read that post, I still agree with it because I’ve had enough results to not be happy with some results, and that was a result I wasn't happy with. And it doesn't matter what other people say or how I got the result. It does get to a point where, if you keep getting a result despite an adversity it’s all well and good, but at the end of the day, I also just wanted a result where it was more simple. And Sunday wasn't really simple, you know. I messed up my start I had these massive gaps to bridge, and then I didn't play the final quite right, even for a medal after all of that.

I was probably being a bit… not optimistic, but I was kind of fantasising about the idea that ‘oh, on Sunday I maybe could have won’, which was probably still a bit ambitious, but I think just fantasising that meant that I could arrive on Wednesday, going, ‘right, well, maybe I can win this one’. No one will know if I could have won or not at Euros. But actually I can decide now. I can try and show everyone that I can win today. It was good timing.

CN: How are you feeling about this season in general? How has it been going and how good have you felt compared to previous seasons?

I feel about the same. At the start, it felt… not harder than ever, but like it felt as fast as ever. And the summer is very long. From my last race in February all the way to my first race again in October, there's a lot that goes on. You just spend all summer going ‘was that the right thing to do?’

The cyclo-cross season such a hard one to periodise because there's always a race, and they're all quite important, and it's just that constant revolving cast of guys on form, guys with problems, Thibau [Nys] coming in, Van der Poel maybe coming in later. It’s just constantly moving, and to pick a goal is really tricky.

What's similar to last year is that I didn't really decide to be this good at this moment. It just kind of happened. But when when that form comes, then you deal with it in a smart way. And I think we've done a really good job of that the last few weeks. We really aimed for Koppenbergcross, and that didn't quite work out physically but when you aim for something, you know that work is going to come through at some point, and it has done in the last couple weeks. And since Middelkerke, I've known that physically I'm there, technically I'm there, tactically there are things to work on, and then you just wait – well, for me it was just waiting until it rained a bit.

CN: The muddy stuff is where you feel you have a big advantage…?

It helps. Once the speeds come down a bit, and once every corner is a little bit more technical, then things just go a bit more in my favour. But the cool thing about this season has been I've been way more competitive on way more different types of courses. When I'm in good shape, it doesn't matter what the course is – if it's fast, if it's sandy or whatever – I’ll be there or thereabouts, but it means that when there's a course that really suits me, then then I've got that extra little edge.

But I'm trying to get away from the obsession with certain courses, because you might be sacrificing an opportunity on a course that you maybe wouldn't have thought you'd be that good at. Last year at the Euros it was a full sand course, bone dry, super fast, 30kph, but I was fighting for a medal. This year, I’m trying to think about it in a different way.

CN: Looking ahead, what what else would you like to get out of the season now?

I mean, there's loads of other races, so that's cool. I want to keep the consistency going. Yesterday was a bit of an outlier in my results – I've got quite a lot of fourths and fifths and sixths, and then I've got this one win – so just to be in in with a shot of winning again would be would be a like realistic goal, and hopefully I can keep this form for as long as I can.

CN: You hinted at it earlier, but is there anything you can tap into now in terms of that winning mindset? You hear of athletes in other sports that have that breakthrough win and something clicks and it sort of opens the floodgates.

Mentally, a bit of the pressure is off because I've proven to everyone and to myself that it's possible, and then yeah, I can turn that into confidence as well. Like, I know how to win, I've worked out how to win on this one specific race, parcours, day… then the puzzle is to do that on another day with different competition, different conditions, with different legs.

As I was saying, it's just another puzzle piece – now there's this piece of the puzzle that says I can win, so how do I do that again? It took like five years to do it, but how do I do it again? I was chatting to my coach this morning, and probably the best thing to do is do nothing. Just do exactly the same and carry on as if I didn't win. Logistically, the training, sleeping, eating, all that stuff needs to be just as good as it was for the last however many years. But the mindset thing, I feel more confident and that can't be a bad thing.

CN: What does the rest of the season hold in terms of your calendar?

need to work out if I'm going to do all the Superprestige races. That wasn't on my calendar, but now I'm leading the series overall, so I need to work out if I focus a bit more on that. I’m probably going to do all of the World Cups. Everyone's got the same puzzle. You can't do everything, so you’ve got to kind of pick and choose. I'll have a better idea after this weekend.

items.title: Which transfers worked in 2026, and which flopped? We analysed the data to find out the real impact of every move
items.author: laura.weislo@futurenet.com (Laura Weislo)
items.content:
Since UCI points have become so important for professional cycling teams, as the three-year totals determine which teams are eligible for the WorldTour, rider transfer have become an even more critical factor in teams' futures.

While the 2026-2027 transfers have yet to be fully completed, we can look back on which of the top acquisitions for the 2026 season have been the biggest successes and which teams suffered the most from not being able to hold onto top talent.

This year was the first of the three-year WorldTour promotion/relegation cycle, with the next relegation coming at the end of the 2028 season, and while the big-budget powerhouses like Red Bull-Bora-Hansgrohe, UAE Team Emirates-XRG and Visma-Lease a Bike might be able to pour millions of euros into acquiring top riders, smaller teams have to be more strategic.

For teams like EF Education-EasyPost, Lotto-Intermarché, NSN and Groupama-FDJ, who were at the bottom quarter of the UCI Team Rankings, their recruitment strategy will be critical for remaining in the WorldTour as upstart ProTeams climb ahead in search of WorldTour promotion in 2029.

Teams have to be in the top 18 of the rankings, calculated by adding the points scored by each team's top 20 riders, to qualify for the WorldTour.

While it's still early days, Pinarello-Q36.5 made enormous strides toward qualifying for the WorldTour, thanks to their top rider Tom Pidcock, but also through smart signings like Quinten Hermans from Alpecin, Aimé De Gendt from Cofidis, Fred Wright from Bahrain Victorious and Chris Harper from Jayco-AlUla.

Pinarello-Q36.5 finished the season as the 12th best team and the top ProTeam of the year, with Tudor next best in 16th place. Both teams will earn automatic invitations to all of the WorldTour races including the Tour de France next year, which will help them earn even more points toward qualifying for the 2029-2031 WorldTour.

On the other side of the equation, Picnic-PostNL had an extremely worrying season. The team lost Tobias Lund Andresen, who went on to have a brilliant year for Decathlon CMA CGM, as well as GC hopeful Oscar Onley, who went to Netcompany Ineos.

Not only did Picnic-PostNl finish dead last of the WorldTour teams in the rankings, they landed in 30th of all teams - on the cusp of not even qualifying for a Grand Tour invitation if they didn't have a WorldTour license that gives them an automatic entry.

If Picnic-PostNL survive the allegations of a toxic culture and continue on toward 2029, the men's team faces a very difficult battle to climb out of the relegation zone since they are already almost 7,000 points behind 18th-placed Cofidis.

Also on the concerning side were Groupama-FDJ, who ended the year in 20th, although not so far behind 18th as to panic just yet.

*The graphics below are all interactive, so you can hover over the bars for more information and in some cases, change the filter to only show transfers.

The Belgian had a banner season, winning the time trial titles at the UCI Road World Championships and European Championships, won two stages of the Tour de France and came second overall, won the Amstel Gold Race, GP de Québec and his fifth Clásica San Sebastián.

Evenepoel benefited greatly from a strong support crew in the Tour de France, where Jai Hindley, Maxim Van Gils, fellow Soudal departure Mattia Cattaneo, and Jan Tratnik were his main support in the mountains.

While he still couldn't match Tadej Pogačar, he did hold off the Slovenian's right-hand man Isaac del Toro to go one place better than his previous best with Soudal-Quickstep in the GC. Evenepoel scored a massive 7,191.61 points this year, with fractions coming from team time trials, and this was the most scored of any of the riders who transfered to new teams in 2026.

The second best rider was Benoit Cosnefroy, who left Decathlon for UAE Team Emirates-XRG. Cosnefroy had a solid year of shorter stage races and one-day classics, taking wins in the Coppa Sabatini and GP du Morbihan, the overall Boucles de la Mayenne, third in Amstel and fourth in La Flèche Wallonne. He didn't race any Grand Tours, but still raked in 2,355.28 points for his team.

Next up in the list was Tobias Lund Andresen who left Picnic-PostNL to join Decathlon, making the most of the switch to win the Cadel Evans Great Ocean Road Race, a stage of the Tour Down Under and Tirreno-Adriatico, and podiums in In Flanders Field and the Copenhagen Sprint. His season might have been an even greater success had he not stopped in June after contracting the Epstein-Barr virus.

Jasper Stuyven's departure from Lidl-Trek for Soudal-Quickstep seemed to rejuvenate the 34-year-old, who claimed the podium in Paris-Roubaix - his best result in a major classic since his 2021 Milan-San Remo win. He also finished in the top 10 in San Remo, the Tour of Flanders, and three stages of the Giro, then capped the year off with second in Paris-Tours for a total of 1,903.88 points.

Of the neo-pros, Jarno Widar (Lotto-Intermarché) topped the list of incoming riders, ending the season with a bang with second behind Pogačar on stage 4 of the Vuelta and two other stage top 10s, then went on to win Tre Valli Varesine and a stage and the overall in the Tour of Guangxi to take in 1,302 points - the second highest tally of his team.

Jakob Omrzel (Bahrain Victorious) wasn't far behind, with seventh overall in the Vuelta and a spectacular stage win at Calar Alto from the breakaway. With a podium in the Tour of Slovenia and a top 10 overall in the Tour of the Alps, Omrzel ended the year with 1,046 points.

A fresh start helped Evenepoel, Cosnefroy and Stuyven in the list of most improved after transferring, with Evenepoel netting 3,064 more points this year than he did in 2025.

Cosnefroy improved by 1,970 after a 2025 season hampered by a knee injury. Slotting into the mix was Anthon Charmig, who moved from XDS Astana to Uno-X Mobility.

Charmig's move to a more familiar team culture may have been a factor behind his great season, with top 10s in the Tour Down Under GC, a stage win in the Tour Auvergne-Rhône-Alpes and podiums in five late-season one-day races including the GP de Québec.

After scoring just a few hundred points with Astana, Charmig ended the year with a massive 1,396 points this year and was ranked 49th in the world. It was a fantastic season for the Dane.

Which teams won the prize for best hirings? It depends a bit on how you measure the success. In terms of net total points - adding points by new arrivals minus the 2026 points scored by riders who left - Red Bull-Bora-Hansgrohe gained the most, largely thanks to Evenepoel, with 8,188 points.

Netcompany Ineos got great results from new hires Dorian Godon - winner of stages in Paris-Nice, Tour de Romandie and Volta a Catalunya - and Oscar Onley, who was sixth overall in the Vuelta a España among other fine results.

Pinarello-Q36.5's tally was the third highest, showing that the ambitious Swiss team are well on their way to qualifying for the WorldTour in 2029. Quinten Hermans steadily picked up points all year, with top finishes in the Renewi Tour and De Brabantse Pijl his most valuable contributions.

While Decathlon CMA CGM earned 6,217 from new arrivals like Tobias Lund Andresen from Picnic-PostNL, sprinter Olav Kooij from Visma, and Riccitello from Israel-Premier Tech, they actually lost out, because their gains did not completely offset their losses of Cosnefroy to UAE and Dorian Godon to Netcompany Ineos.

If we look at the percentage of points gained by incoming riders and ignore the total points, NSN Cycling tops the list. After changing their identity from Israel-Premier Tech, NSN Cycling earned almost 41% of their total points from incoming riders such as Biniam Girmay, Lewis Askey and Alessandro Pinarello.

Even though they ended the season with a net positive transfer score after losing Derek Gee-West to Lidl-Trek and Matthew Riccitello to Decathlon, their returning riders like Corbin Strong and Marco Frigo had relatively lacklustre seasons and the team actually fell five places in the UCI Team Rankings.

Red Bull-Bora-Hansgrohe had 37% of their total come from incoming riders, mainly Evenepoel but also solid results from neo-pro Luke Tuckwell - second overall in the Tour Auvergne-Rhône-Alpes and leader for two stages, and Gianni Vermeersch who had a solid Classics campaign after leaving Alpecin, with fifth in Strade Bianche his most notable result.

Drilling down to perhaps the most important factor in the UCI Team Rankings is the team's position and whether it improved or fell with the team's new composition in 2026. The above graph charts the percentage of points scored by incoming riders, the team's change in rank relative to 2025 and the total points scored by new arrivals.

Pinarello-Q36.5 both had a large portion of their points come from transfers and the biggest gain in position, gaining seven places and rocketing into the top 18 at 12th.

The merger between Lotto and Intermarché was the main factor behind their rise in the rankings from 23rd and 24th for the two parent teams to 16th. Jarno Widar, who graduated from Lotto's devo team, was the top earner with his victories in Guangxi and Tre Valli Varesine.

Decathlon CMA CGM ended the year with a gain of three spots in the UCI Team Rankings thanks in large part to their young phenom Paul Seixas and reliable GC man Felix Gall, even if their net transfer value was in the negative territory.

Soudal-Quickstep, but losing Evenepoel, slid five positions to tenth place, and while they have to rebuild from here, they're not in much danger of relegation.

The same can't be said for Picnic-PostNL. This graph really emphasises their terrible year - they dropped a massive 13 spots and had very few points from incoming riders, showing no positive direction in any of the measures. They only won three races all year, and only a single WorldTour stage by Frits Biesterbos in the Tour of Guangxi.

The net total of a team's transfer strategy doesn't tell the whole story, however, because one big signing like Evenepoel can overshadow a wider roster shift that can bode well for the future. Even the average points can fall victim to the same problem of outliers.

The median score can be a better measure, unless there were very few new riders in a team.

Bahrain Victorious seem to have done well in most measures: they had a net gain of almost 2,300 points, a gain of three positions in the UCI Team Rankings going from 10th to seventh, and the highest median points per new rider.

That included performances by Giro d'Italia stage winner Alec Segaert, neo-pro Jakob Omrzel, who won a stage and finished seventh overall in the Vuelta a España, and consistent seasons from Pau Miquel and Alessandro Borgo.

Lidl-Trek, while not getting the most out of Juan Ayuso, still earned over 1,700 points from the Spaniard and almost 1,300 from Derek Gee-West, and good value from Max Walscheid and Matteo Sobrero for the second highest median score.

Once again, Picnic-PostNL are dead last, showing that their new hires just aren't paying off, with the exception of Biesterbos.

Looking at the points scored by riders leaving a team tells an interesting story. Soudal-Quickstep of course, with Evenepoel's departure, bled out in 2026 gaining only 3,806 points from incoming riders but seeing departing riders score over 8,000 points between Evenepoel and Luke Lamperti's haul for EF Education-EasyPost.

However, between Paul Magnier and Tim Merlier, the team softened the blow, holding onto the top 10 in the team rankings.

Lotto-Intermarché suffered by losing Girmay, winner of the Clásica Almeria, a stage of the Belgium Tour and third in the Tour de France points classification with five top-10 finishes in stages. Their story is complicated by the fact that Lotto and Intermarché merged before 2026, so their departing riders' total is inflated as half the team left.

But Picnic-PostNL's total is not. They lost Lund, Onley and Kevin Vermaerke and only picked up a significant number of points from bringing Biesterbos in from the BEAT Continental team. The 24-year-old was their second-top scorer behind Pavel Bittner, who is leaving for Pinarello-Q36.5 in 2027.

There were also a few transfers that didn't quite work out as expected - with Juan Ayuso most notably struggling to match his 2025 performance with UAE Team Emirates and ending up with almost 900 fewer points than last year, but it could have been much higher had it not been for bad luck.

Oscar Onley and Kévin Vauquelin's totals were even more significantly lower at 1,545 and 1,409 less, respectively.

Onley traded a fourth place overall in the Tour de France last year for sixth place overall after an early crash and illness in the Vuelta. He missed the Tour because he injured his shoulder in a crash in the Tour Auvergne-Rhône-Alpes. Vauquelin finished fourth in Paris-Nice but had an unremarkable Tour de France.

Fred Wright took a while to get going after switching from Bahrain Victorious to Pinarello-Q36.5 after suffering a bizarre infection due to a thorn getting stuck in his knee during a training camp in Chile but ended the season with some solid one-day race results including the British road title.

items.title: Ferrari's Leclerc-Hamilton problem is far from solved
items.author: Josh Suttill
items.content:
Don't be fooled by Ferrari's Formula 1 drivers playing nicely in Brazil; there are still very real tensions between Charles Leclerc and Lewis Hamilton.

The drivers and team principal Fred Vasseur got together in Brazil to try to talk things through after Hamilton's extraordinary criticism of Leclerc following their victory-losing Mexico run-in.

That meeting proved constructive, and Leclerc and Hamilton were very well-behaved during the Brazilian Grand Prix, even following team orders and leaving each other plenty of room, unlike in Mexico.

Hamilton's summary was: "Everything's good. Fred brought us together. Fred was great in the meeting. And then he just left me and Charles to just give our points.

"We both had a really good, open discussion. And it's all good now. We'll just move on."

But you can't compare Mexico and Brazil, so Vasseur didn't bother reaching for what would have been an easy pat-on-the-back.

"You can't compare the two situations," Vasseur said, in respect of Leclerc and Hamilton's cordiality on-track at Interlagos.

"Honestly, we had a good discussion on Friday. We cleared the situation. We did a good reset on the mindset.

"They left my room joking together. It's good. I hope that it will last, to stay like this."

All Vasseur can do for now is "hope" it lasts because that Brazil fight was only ever going to be for minor points-paying positions, not a race win or a podium.

So there's every reason to believe that when the Ferrari is back fighting for wins, be it in Las Vegas or Qatar or Abu Dhabi, Hamilton and Leclerc are going to be back fighting tooth and nail.

After all, Leclerc admitted post-meeting: "Of course there is tension, of course we want to finish ahead of each other, and sometimes we are not going to do things right, and it's OK sometimes to disagree on the way you see things.

"But at the same time discussing about those helps a whole lot."

In light of the Leclerc-Hamilton tensions, Leclerc's ex-team-mate at Ferrari Carlos Sainz was asked about his time with Leclerc.

Hamilton had, after all, pointed to Leclerc's time alongside Sainz and Sebastian Vettel as evidence that he races his team-mates harder.

"I have relatively good memories of my time with Charles and the fights we had," Sainz said in Brazil.

"It is true that when you're fighting for wins, there's always more pressure, more things down the line. So you become naturally a bit more selfish than when you are fighting in the midfield for a P8 or a P9.

"It's more difficult maybe to follow exactly the ideal situation that the team would like you to follow, because there's a win down the line. There was wins down the line back then, but I always respected Charles. He always respected me. We never had contacts or anything like this. We just had strong fights. You remember Monza, Vegas. There was plenty of hot moments during the year.

"What was difficult more was the fanbase. The PR and the fanbase was really ignited back then, and it was very polarised between Charles and me. And I remember suffering a bit from the very hardcore fans of Charles insulting or wishing me bad.

"Maybe some Italian media also saying that I was not being enough of a number two when I needed to be, and vice-versa whenever Charles had to do it.

"So it's more the pressure surrounding Ferrari, that involves Ferrari, than the actual issues that I had with Charles, which were always resolved that same night when we called each other with a more cold head and we always managed to find the solution and the way forward."

Sainz felt it is an inevitable problem with having two equals in the same team.

"I cannot remember no Formula 1 team that has had two good drivers fighting at the front that haven't had issues when fighting for wins," Sainz added.

"You can choose whether to have a number two as a second driver, or you can have two good drivers that will create those issues. But you cannot have one without the other, in my opinion. And you will never have one without the other.

"Maybe in Ferrari it gets a bit exacerbated with everything that involves Ferrari, but I cannot remember a moment where this hasn't happened. It happened in Mercedes. It happened in McLaren the last few years. It happened in Ferrari.

"So I don’t know when it hasn't happened. It is part of Formula 1. And if you are a team principal and you know you're going to have two great drivers, you're always going to have that issue.

"I don't think you can ever calm those two guys 100% down and expect them not to go for a move for a race win."

Why Leclerc-Hamilton is different

There are some parallels to the tensions in 2019 when Leclerc managed to steal Ferrari away from four-time world champion Sebastian Vettel as a 21-year-old. This piece by Mark Hughes still stands as an excellent account of that.

Back then, the drivers were 'free to race', the team principal (Mattia Binotto) tried to play things fairly, the drivers were close enough in performance to routinely be near each other on track, and there was a huge battle for supremacy.

Leclerc ultimately won that battle convincingly, with Sainz brought into replace Vettel, but never as an equal to Leclerc. (That didn't mean he was a dutiful number two either. He was too quick for that.)

Leclerc and Sainz had their flashpoints, but ultimately things never uncontrollably spilt over for one good reason: Leclerc was ahead of Sainz around two-thirds of the time.

The dynamic therefore was very different: Leclerc even ended up helping Sainz to the only non-Verstappen victory of 2023 in Singapore. That was evidence of Leclerc playing the long game, knowing a small sacrifice there would only strengthen his position once Ferrari had a title-challenging car.

There was ultimately enough of a performance gap for there never to be too much needle between them. Leclerc didn't see Sainz as a threat to his position as Ferrari's spearhead. He was right, as Ferrari chose to replace Sainz with Hamilton just a few months after that Singapore win.

And it's no coincidence that in 2025, there being a clear performance gap between Leclerc and Hamilton meant there wasn't much needle between them.

Suddenly they're very closely matched in 2026, and the Leclerc-Vettel era tension is immediately re-exposed because now there is a threat to Leclerc's position. Leclerc was previously fairly comfortable, like Vettel was in 2015-18 as the focal point of the team, with team-mate Kimi Raikkonen very much a support act.

Now there is an active battle for supremacy. If Ferrari improves its power unit and has a title-challenging car next year, both Hamilton and Leclerc want to be the one leading that charge.

It's why the prospect of Ferrari's Brazil meeting being any kind of full stop on its Leclerc-Hamilton problem is absolute nonsense.

That's not going to change until Leclerc has destroyed another world champion - as he did to Vettel - or until he's the one destroyed by a team-mate.

items.title: Pochettino’s Chelsea maelstrom the best yardstick for what lies ahead at United
items.author: Andrew Beasley
items.content:
Argentinian oversaw high-scoring games in his one Chelsea season and Opta predicts his Manchester United side will move upfield quicker than that team

Among the 20 managers with more than 290 matches in the Premier League, only the five “big beasts” of Alex Ferguson, Arsène Wenger, José Mourinho, Jürgen Klopp and Pep Guardiola have better points-per-game averages than Mauricio Pochettino. He is an elite manager.

Pochettino took over Southampton midway through their first season back in the top flight (2012-13) after the club spent seven years in the lower leagues. In his only full campaign, they finished eighth. He led Tottenham to second in 2016-17, third in the seasons either side, and reached the 2019 Champions League final. His presence lifted those clubs.
