PHD chemistry and three types of sand – Inside the CeramicSpeed chain lubricant test labs
items.author: thomas.wieckowski@futurenet.com (Tom Wieckowski)
items.content:
Cyclists have been applying lubricants to their bicycle chains for well over a century. From the invention of 3-in-1 oil in 1894 to condition-specific wet and dry formulations, through to hot waxing and the performance-focused, watt-saving lubricants we have today.

There are now countless products promising an increase in speed, quietness and longevity. Currently, no industry-standard test procedures exist for chain lubricants and waxes, and what is the best thing to test? There are established big names, but how can you tell an effective product from one that might actually do your drivetrain harm?

CeramicSpeed is one brand that formulates and tests all of its own chain waxes and lubricants in-house. A fact which possibly draws less attention than the brand's more visible high-end ceramic bearings and OSPW pulley wheel systems.

I visited the CeramicSpeed headquarters in Holstebro, Denmark, where the brand has dedicated chain-lubricant formulation and test labs in an attempt to answer a few of the questions the chain lube nerd in me had, and to learn more about how you go about formulating an effective chain lubricant or wax, testing it and bringing it to market.

The origins of the modern-day chain waxing revolution lie with Jason Smith’s Friction Facts chain lubricant and testing business, which carried out some of the very first, if not the first, dedicated drivetrain friction testing over a decade ago.

CeramicSpeed acquired FrictionFacts in 2016, including at least one of its test machines, and then built on Smith’s original UFO product foundation. Smith joined the business as well, and later worked on the Driven chainless drivetrain project, but is no longer involved.

Product development and rigorous testing are a cornerstone of the CeramicSpeed product philosophy. The brand commits plenty of time to formulating and testing chain products.

Various brands carry out their own lubricant testing; some do none. It varies, and more than one brand markets its products as the fastest. ZeroFriction, an Australian independent testing company, is a reference point for many who are interested in lubricants and testing, but a lot happens behind closed doors.

CeramicSpeed chain products begin life in the brand's lab. Glass flasks line a wall, and at the end of a workbench topped with several machines that look a bit like microscopes, there’s a cabinet full of the base ingredients used to produce chain lubes and wax. This being Denmark early in the year, the carpet of snow on the ground outside matches the colour of the product in some of the bottles today.

Lina Søbjerg Madsen, a PHD chemist, and Michael Pedersen, Development Engineer, have both been with CeramicSpeed for the best part of a decade and form the backbone of the brand's wax and lubricant development and testing programme. If you have used a CeramicSpeed lube or wax product in that time, they will have developed and tested it.

CeramicSpeed wax and lube products are both wax-based. Hot melt wax is a blend of pure waxes, including what Søbjerg Madsen tells me, with a grin, is her 'secret ingredient'.

When it comes to a drip chain lubricant in a bottle, Ceramicspeed uses wax, emulsifiers, a corrosion inhibitor to protect the chain, which it claims not every brand uses, and demineralised water as the carrier, which is what, as the name suggests, helps carry the wax lubricant itself deep into your chain links, where it can do its work and protect the chain.

Drip lubricants are mixed thoroughly using machines, heated, and then cooled. Today's formulations are water-based, but the original carrier fluid for the first UFO Drip was kerosene, which was known to melt bottle nozzles over time due to its aggressive nature.

The water-based carrier evaporates, leaving behind the wax. Oil-based drip lubricants tend to become dirtier in use because contamination is suspended within the oil, which remains on the chain.

Charged with developing CeramicSpeed’s chain lube offerings, Søbjerg Madsen begins by explaining that it’s not possible to have one product that’s the best at everything.

“What people need to understand is that there are over 1000 different waxes; there are synthetic and natural products, and each of them has different properties. She explains.

“So when sales suggests a new lubricant or a new product, my main goal is to ask, 'What kind of properties do you want?’, because you can't have everything.

“The first part is getting the wax composition with the properties that I would like, and once that's done, then I need to find a way to keep it in this water solution, and also get the shelf life correct, and that's a really difficult task.” Søbjerg Madsen explains.

A product's composition depends on the desired properties. Is longevity the priority, or is all-out efficiency the goal? Something that lasts for a thousand kilometres may very well not be the fastest option.

CeramicSpeed's approach is that a one-size-fits-all product isn't ideal for chain treatments. The first wet lube, for instance, went through 300 experiments to arrive at the desired composition.

Cyclists, or at least road cyclists with a focus on performance, often look for what's fastest, or what saves watts, but there's more to it than that. Making a quality product that performs for the most amount of riders, across different regions, climates and weather systems is a tricky ask.

CeramicSpeed offers three drip products: All Conditions, Wet, and Indoor and the range was overhauled this year and given a new look.

All Conditions and Speed Wax are the best bet for speed; Wet lasts longer and protects your chain in the rain, and Indoor doesn't shed like a regular wax, making it useful for the velodrome or home training. The new Ultra Endurance Wax doesn't focus on low friction, a first for the brand; its priority is high durability and consistent performance over hundreds of kilometres.

It is 'stickier'. It might not be the quickest option for a road race, but it will protect a chain for hundreds of kilometres off-road in a gravel race, for example. A super-fast chain wax or lube's benefits will be null and void if it's gone after 2 hours of hard use.

The brand's chain lubricants are developed in small batches in the lab and produced in volumes of up to two litres. These samples are used for the brand's testing and by test riders.

The brand now also has an in-house production facility where it can produce 50- 300 kg of drip product in a batch, allowing them to control the process.

Søbjerg Madsen explains that this close proximity means it can be easy to address issues that may arise from production at scale.

“Sometimes, because it's chemistry, and chemistry can be unpredictable when you scale up, we'll see some issues where I have to correct something, then when they say go, they are ready to produce and put it in bottles,” she explains.

Shelf life is another factor when it comes to our chain lubricant; top tip: don’t leave the cap off your water-based drip chain wax, as the water will evaporate over time.

CeramicSpeed aims for a two-year product shelf life, and needs to ensure a product doesn't solidify in the bottle. Søbjerg Madsen explains that a drip lube which separates in the bottle is a poor sign, something to look for when you are next in the bike shop buying chain lube.

"That's a very poor sign; it's a sign that it's unstable, and the product development didn't do a good enough job.

"Every time I make the sample, I put it in the incubator at 40 degrees. It stays there for three months, and if it doesn't solidify or separate, then we say we have a shelf life of two years," she says.

After nearly a decade, it's clear the pair have a strong feel for what's needed, but verification from the test lab's machines and Pedersen's experience and feel inform the direction Søbjerg Madsen needs to take at times.

"When I make the first wax compositions, and I think 'Okay, this might be interesting,' then I'll make a test chain for Michael and ask him to do an experiment to measure the watts, because then I have an idea. If it's really high, then I need to do something to make it lower," she explains.

The testing lab and three different kinds of sand

The lubricant and wax formulations are designed, and then the testing phase takes around six months on average, though the brand is always busy testing different things, including the competition, and running experiments.

Engineer Pedersen has tested a lot of products in general in the lab, including over 800 chains; the 11-speed Shimano Dura-Ace chain is held in particularly high regard. If you are running 11-speed Shimano, buy yourself a Dura-Ace chain.

CeramicSpeed uses a combination of internal and external test riders. This includes company founder and CEO Jacob Csizmadia himself; we pass a few of his stealth all-black bikes in the corridor on our way to the lab.

The test lab is a fairly small, brightly lit room that is lined with workbenches. Many of which are topped with testing machines, which in different ways all vaguely resemble a bicycle drivetrain.

There are five chain testing machines, which all serve a different purpose; There's the original Friction Facts testing machine, a clean conditions test machine, a wet conditions test machine, a machine to add water and sand contaminants together and the brand's latest baby, the Full Load Watt Tester machine (FLWT); a larger unit, which runs as a complete drivetrain, whilst adding sand and water and measuring friction. This machine has been designed to take the brand's testing to the next level.

CeramicSpeed measures friction in watts by using torque sensors. The durability of the chain treatment is also monitored, but chain wear specifically is not, though it can be as part of a specific extra-long extreme test.

The Friction Facts test machine was the original, weighting a single-speed arrangement at 250 watts of load in a clean environment. It's a style of machine being used by other brands to test as well, but it isn't a full drivetrain and can skew results because the chain is in tension pretty much the whole time due to there being no derailleur.

A Tribology test for friction rates called a Pin and Disc test also exists, and whilst it can be performed to an ISO standard, it isn't specific to bicycle drivetrains or modern wax formulas. CeramicSpeed don't consider it to be a worthwhile testing avenue to go down.

For years, only clean-conditions testing could be done, but as Søbjerg Madsen points out, unless you are riding in a velodrome environment, "we all know even on a hot summer day, it's not completely clean conditions," meaning dust and other contaminants are still present.

A machine that could add contamination was required to mimic real-world conditions. The wet conditions test machine was also developed, but adding only water could only tell so much.

"We could only add water, and a lot of water, and what does that really simulate in the real world?" Søbjerg Madsen says. Every cyclist knows a wet, rainy day comes with all sorts of grit, dirt, and mud that also interact with a chain.

CeramicSpeed has now developed a machine capable of adding contamination and water. The FLWT machine is run using four different protocols that simulate different conditions over five hours; to standardise things, because, as the pair point out, you could end up just testing forever.

These test protocols are as follows:

- Clean test without contamination.- Tests with water added every five minutes. - Dry test with sand added every five minutes.- Extreme test with water and sand added every 15 minutes.

The brand also uses three different types of sand from around the world in testing because, naturally, it varies all over the world. Sand from Australia, Denmark and America is used. The sands all differ; the one from Colorado in the US is very fine and dusty, the sample from Australia has more clay, and the Danish sand has more 'fine particles'; using it consistently allows for repeatable testing.

The FLWT machine uses a motor to power a drivetrain at a load of 250 watts (though this can be altered) and advanced torque sensors on the input and output axles to measure the wattage difference; custom test software has also been written in-house to calculate the test results.

CeramicSpeed runs various tests, and the brand was careful not to give me everything; it's a competitive area, so we couldn't dive into all of the test data, graphs and findings. The brand has published some test results on its site for its chain lubricants.

Generally, though, tests last five hours, and multiple runs of each test are completed for validation. When test graphs are produced, they show a break in time, an optimal running period and a decline in performance due to wear and/or abrasion from the test contaminants.

The FLWT can also be remotely controlled and has a built-in horn to warn colleagues that a test is about to start when the engineers are working remotely.

There is even a microphone to monitor the changing sound of a chain's treatment as testing progresses and a lubricant 'wears in'. The sound a chain is making can tell the engineers a lot, and plenty of riders recognise a change in sound as a reminder to re-lube or re-wax their chains.

Apparatus in workshops to break in freshly waxed chains is also getting more complex; the brand's advice: re-install your freshly waxed chain, work it by hand a little if needed and go ride it; it will settle down and go quiet soon enough.

"We know from the industry that there are a lot of people who are looking into this (an FLWT-style machine), but we have also realised that the problem is getting reproducible data. says Søbjerg Madsen.

"We really need to be sure that what we are measuring is correct,"

The team admit that they are still learning the machine, and are aiming to measure very fine differences consistently in order to be as accurate as possible, in part because differences between competitor products are very small.

No lubricant test standard exists in the bike industry, and you can't really just go and buy a test machine. This means brands are free to present their testing in whichever way suits them best.

"Customers and the companies are saying, 'Well, of course, you're just designing your test to make yours look best,' and that's what everybody is doing, because there is no standard.

"That's what everybody is doing; they are making their own test, and then, of course, they look best, but what Michael and I are really doing, and it's easy for us to say, is that we are really trying to make tests that mimic the real world. It's much easier to optimise something if you have a standard test to do it," says Søbjerg Madsen

The brand is comparing against the competition, but appears to be doing it fairly, setting up and testing competitor products to spec, as Søbjerg Madsen explains.

"If we're doing comparison tests on one of our competitors, we do a lot of work to test it at what they recommend.

"We are not just trying to make it look awful. Sometimes we find that, well, this lubricant is actually really good under these conditions, and then, of course, as a chemist and scientist, I'm thinking, 'okay, what do they do that's really good, and how can I optimise mine to get the same performance?"

The clue is in the name: with CeramicSpeed, the brand is all about speed and low friction; however, its efforts with chain treatments, drip and hot wax go beyond being able to say 'ours is fastest'. It's a statement the engineers do not make themselves during my visit.

Cyclists can make an informed decision on what they might think the best chain product for them is. The brand of drivetrain you run will affect efficiency, as will how well a lubricant is applied and maintained. If you want to maintain the best possible performance, don't skip the re-waxing, cleaning or reapplication, and if that isn't for you, find something that lasts a long time.

Though no official industry test standards exist, inter-brand chain lube test result announcements can feel like a fight for supremacy at times.

It's clear CeramicSpeed is committed to testing and developing the best possible product. Whilst its product has competitive low-friction or speed levels, there's more to a good chain lube or wax than just being quick.

items.title: Knicks Bulletin: ‘It’s gonna be hard to find minutes at times for Mikal’
items.author: Antonio Losada
items.content:
The Cavaliers did on Wednesday what they do best: win meaningless, regular-season games.

The Knicks, meanwhile, handed out a dub and ate a loss on purpose on their way to find their best-working lineups for when winning, you know, actually matters.

Here’s the latest from MSG on a rare off day.

“We’ll learn from this game, and keep it moving.”

On why Bridges remains a starter despite his shooting slump:

“Mikal is a starter. And so it’s not a question of that. He’s like a lot of players: They’ve had their good moments and their not so good moments. And Mikal has a proven track record of playing at a pretty high level as a starter in this league.

“So, for me to make a quote-unquote ‘panic decision’ and change it right now — we’re 10 games in or whatever we are. I’m not feeling it. So I’m good.”

On the Knicks’ defensive physicality and ability to defend without fouling:

“Just our level of physicality. Our level of physicality without fouling. Because you can be over the top, grabbing and pushing and holding, but our guys, they’re doing their work early. They’re doing their work early and they’re being real physical about it without putting their hands on guys. When you do that and you do that for close to 48 minutes, you usually get good results. And our guys are doing it.”

On the defensive intensity of Landry Shamet and Miles McBride:

“I think our physicality on the defensive end of the floor is at a pretty high level. And they [are doing] it the right way. They’re doing it without fouling, which is a lot of fun to watch. The point of attack with Landry and Deuce, especially, on the ball, is unbelievable.”

On Josh Hart’s perimeter defense and the importance of his return:

“He’s tremendous on the ball. In pick-and-roll situations, we always want our point of confrontation, especially against guys that shoot the ball at the 3-point line, Josh is really good at that. He’s really good at leading with his chest. And he’s strong. He’s a strong guy that knows the league, he knows the players very well.

“His impact when it comes to guarding the ball, on the perimeter especially, is something that you always miss.”

On the Knicks’ defensive communication, rebounding and improved pick-and-roll coverage:

“Their level of communication is high. Their ability to box out is high. Their ability to get back in transition is high. We were hurting in the pick-and-roll game defensively, but we’ve done a better job because the point of attack has been good and our guy guarding the screener has been great, too.”

On Mikal Bridges and Josh Hart losing minutes to Shamet and McBride:

“It’s gonna be hard to find minutes at times for Mikal. And maybe even at times for Josh. Because those two guys [McBride and Shamet] are playing at a pretty high level.

“Part of it is we got two guys that are playing really well in Landry and Deuce. And so it’s hard. It’s going to be hard to find minutes at times for Mikal — and maybe even at times for Josh, because those two guys are playing at a pretty high level, and not just on the offense of the floor but defensively, too.”

On the Knicks’ defensive struggles against Cleveland and his decision to keep playing Shamet and McBride:

“I mean, this is one of our worst defensive games overall that we’ve had. In the past five or six games we’ve been playing really well at that end of the floor, but they got loose tonight.

“And Landry and Deuce have been a big part of what we’ve done defensively. So if they’re playing at a high level, I’ve? got to keep trying to find ways to get those guys on the floor.”

On taking responsibility for keeping the Knicks in their defensive blitz against Donovan Mitchell too long:

“We blitzed Donovan in the second half and that fourth quarter. Give Donovan credit, he did a nice job making the right play out of it. … I kept us in the blitz a little too long, and I should have taken us out of the blitz. That part is on me.

“I kept us in the blitz a little too long. I should have taken us out of the blitz. So that part is on me and I gotta be better helping our group in that area.”

On the Knicks’ curious lack of free-throw attempts:

“[Cleveland] had 14 more free-throw attempts than us, four more offensive rebounds than us and two less turnovers. When that happens versus a good team, it’s gonna be hard to win the game.

“At one time, the free-throw advantage was 18-3. That’s not why we lost the game, but you just hope to get a little bit better whistle when you’re playing a good team like that, because it’s already hard enough to go win a game.”

On Brunson receiving no free-throw attempts despite playing nearly 35 minutes:

“Jalen plays 34 minutes or almost 35 minutes and he has zero free-throw attempts. That’s pretty alarming. I’m not sure how or why it’s that way. I know at one time, the free throw advantage was 18-3. That’s not why we lost the game, but you just hope to get a little bit better whistle when you’re playing a good team like that, because it’s already hard enough to go win a game. That was part of the reason why we lost the possession game. … James Harden had a great game as well. James shot as many free throws as our whole team.”

On Andre Drummond helping replace Mitchell Robinson’s offensive rebounding:

“Andre’s done a fantastic job in that area, as an individual. He’s not Mitch, nobody would compare him to Mitch, but he’s brought a dimension to the table that we really like. He’s always been a great offensive rebounder, and he’s showing it now as an individual.”

On the Knicks’ assistant coaches emphasizing offensive rebounding and transition defense:

“They’re handling the offensive duties and they’ve been emphasizing the crash areas. And they’ve done a great job — a fantastic job — of coaching our group, in that area. So our guys have a really good understanding of when to go and when not to go and how to go so we don’t get beat in transition.”

On the Knicks failing to execute in crucial moments against Cleveland:

“We were in it. But just timely stops and timely buckets were needed.”

On Cleveland’s defensive adjustments and his failure to respond quickly enough:

“You gotta give them a lot of credit. It’s something I’ll be a little more prepared for. I just didn’t adjust in-game as fast as I wanted to. I was still able to make plays, but not enough to win.”

On needing to be more aggressive even if it means making mistakes:

“From how we started the game to how we finished it, just from my end, I can’t be hesitant. I can’t be a little stagnant at times. It puts my team at a disadvantage, so I just have to be more aggressive in my mistakes, if I’m making any. I just need to have a little more aggression.”

On supporting Mikal Bridges despite his struggles and criticism from outside the team:

“No matter what’s going on, with what people are saying or anything, the people in this room have his back night in and night out. We see the work he puts into his game. We see the time that he puts in. When you’re doing the right things day in and day out, things will eventually fall in your favor. So just giving him support, giving him confidence every single day, regardless of what the noise is on the outside. That’s our brother, and we’re going to keep it that way.”

On controlling what he can after receiving no free-throw attempts against Cleveland:

“I just gotta control what I can control, and keep it at that.”

On taking greater rebounding responsibility following Mitchell Robinson’s departure:

“When you lose a great offensive rebounder like Mitchell Robinson, you got to pick up the slack. Of course, we have one of the best rebounders of the generation in Andre Drummond. But I want to do my part, and one of the ways I can impact winning and help our team tremendously on a nightly basis is make sure they don’t get second-chance points and also we get second-chance points.”

On the difficulty of defending James Harden after his 32-point performance:

“MVP, scoring champ. He’s a tough matchup for anybody in this league. You gotta tip your hat to him.”

On the uncalled goaltending on Peyton Watson’s block:

“I thought it was a goaltend. The guys behind the bench said that as well.”

On James Harden and Donovan Mitchell adjusting to the Knicks’ defensive blitz:

“James has been doing this a long time. Donovan’s been doing this a long time. They probably got a little comfortable. At the end of the day, it was a one-possession game, and we could have shored up a few things, probably, that would have helped us keep it a little tighter and given us a chance to win. But give them credit, because they knew what we were doing and took advantage of it.”

On his offensive rebounding prowess:

“I just got a knack for it.”

On the Knicks collectively replacing Mitchell Robinson’s offensive rebounding contributions:

“I think a lot of that is effort. And just doing it. A lot of us are crashing. You see guys like Deuce going in for those plays. Everybody, honestly. Picking up where we left off last year. We had a guy (Robinson) who was able to grab a lot of offensive boards, get us extra possessions. So all of us had to kind of step up and do that. But Dre has been doing a great job of rebounding, getting us extra possessions. Kicking it out and finding his way.”

items.title: MET’s New Manta 3 Aero Helmet Promises 6 Free Watts. Here Is What the Data Actually Says.
items.author: Josh Ross
items.content: The Italian brand finally details the tech behind Tadej Pogačar’s WorldTour helmet. We break down the F1-inspired aero claims, the 250-gram footprint, and why its 5-star safety rating matters more than ever.

items.title: MET Manta 3 review: The all-conquering helmet of the UAE team has finally launched, but just how good is it really?
items.author: andy@atpperformance.uk (Andy Turner)
items.content:
£299.99 / $375 / €330

249g size Medium, 250g claimed

Small, Medium, and Large

Absolute White, Matte Black, White Black, Glossy Red, Luminous Blue Matte Gloss

The MET Manta 3 helmet is not strictly a new helmet. It first broke cover in early 2026 when it was worn on debut by Tadej Pogačar to win yet another monument at Milan-San Remo.

Since then, it has been used nearly exclusively by Team UAE-Emirates-XRG, taking the Tour de France yet again, more Monuments, and another men’s World Title this time for Brandon McNulty.

Today, however, the helmet officially launches, which means we get to learn a little more about it. We have been testing it on the road in the run-up to launch to see how it performs.

Designed using MET’s own wind tunnel, The Tube, with a tagline of ‘Aero is Proven', takes the approach of tangible performance gains, from decreased drag to increased ventilation and reduced weight, all while maintaining safety thanks to in-depth analysis of over 140 crashed helmets.

However, the price has also increased, and we have yet to test it ourselves in the wind tunnel to see how it stacks up against the best aero helmets, but initial real-world testing of the helmet so far has been mostly very promising.

Design and specifications

The main design point of the new MET Menta 3 places a heavy focus on aerodynamics. To do this, MET uses its own proprietary wind tunnel, The Tube.

This is also the wind tunnel that sponsored teams use for testing new road and time trial helmets with riders to ensure there is good correlation between CFD modelling and then actual on-person testing, something we’ve seen the importance of with our own wind tunnel helmet testing.

MET has shared one test figure: 6 watts faster than the old Manta 2, but does not state at what speed this is. Likely 45-50kph given the speeds of WorldTour road races, and these speeds tend to give larger watt differences.

MET states that the Manta 3 topped the testing against benchmark competitors. This figure is a reasonable one for those speeds, based on our CN Labs helmet testing as well, and certainly it features a host of design features that lend themselves to strong aero performance. The helmet is narrower and longer than the previous version, and more contoured to divert airflow down the back of the rider rather than create low-pressure turbulence at the rear of the helmet.

The helmet looks similar to the likes of the Trek Ballista and Oakley Velo Mach, both helmets that did well in our testing especially when fitted to a rider model in a more aggressive breakaway position.

However, this helmet features noticeably more vents than these options. Ventilation was another key target for MET; it states the new Manta has 10% better ventilation than the predecessor.

Apparantly this was tested using a thermal viewer and capture system with a copper-coated head model. No further details were provided, as that likely covers some trade secrets.

This increased ventilation comes from more frontal vents, the new brow vent borrowed from the Trenta Gen 2, and greater channelling internally into exhausts. This is a similar system to the POC Procen Air, which I find very well-vented at speed thanks to inlets and large channels inside.

MET uses a double deck at the rear of the helmet, both to increase the airflow and heat exhaustion, and to help channel that air over the back of the rider.

Safety is also key here, with the helmet getting a 5-star Virginia Tech Helmet Lab rating. MIPS Air Node Pro is used inside for rotational impact protection, and it also helps keep the weight low at 250g claimed for a medium, 249g on our scales.

All the EPS foam is also wrapped and protected by the polycarbonate shell, while the Safe-T fit system ensures a secure fit around the head and across the cradle and straps. To test the safety of the helmet, 142 crashed helmets from sponsored teams were analysed, along with 745 test impacts across different angles and velocities, and counting.

At present, colour options include matte back, absolute white, gloss red, and team colourways. Sizes are S, M and L. DualGel front pad and USB LED light are additional accessories that can be purchased separately.

Something I really wasn’t a fan of with the previous generation Manta was that the helmet felt to be rather tight on the sides of my head. I also found this on the first-generation Trenta.

With the latest Manta, I am glad to say that the fit has been greatly improved, and it is a lot less narrow on the sides relative to the length. It does this while still incorporating MIPS technology in the form of Air Node. This is widely used across a lot of road helmets now and has a good reputation for getting a good score in the Virginia Tech Helmet Safety Rating. Indeed, the new Trenta helmet is one of the highest-scoring road helmets that has been tested there and features similar technology.

Testing the helmet, the hot weather of the summer has gone, but there have still been a few days with low 20°C temperatures to test out the ventilation. Having had a helmet sent to test in the matte Black colour, there is a degree of heat radiation absorption, and the helmet does get warm to the touch in indirect sunlight.

I much prefer helmets in light colour options for this reason. However, the ventilation is greatly improved compared to the previous helmet. The front vents are larger, while the internal channelling is deeper to allow for a greater degree of movement of air within the helmet.

This also means that at speed there is a good amount of hot air that exits the rear in the exhaust vents. This effect is most felt at speeds above 35 km an hour, though, with professional road racing speeds of 45 km an hour making this helmet incredibly airy.

However, at lower speeds with reduced airflow, the lack of vents on the top of the helmet does mean that it can get quite stuffy, especially when climbing at low speeds and high outputs. This is a helmet designed to go fast.

Another new feature is the brow venting, as seen on the new Trenta helmet. It does a good job at reducing the amount of heat buildup around your forehead, but being someone who runs quite warm, I still found the over longer rides I had sweat dripping into my eyes.

At present, the only helmets that have eliminated this are the Giro Eclipse Pro and Aries, as the brow pad padding features a silicone bead which diverts the sweat to the side of your face.

However, MET does state that a MET DualGel front pad is available; I have not tested this yet, but a gel design may help disperse sweat to the side of the brow and away from the eyes.

In terms of the aerodynamic performance, it is difficult to say, as we have yet to test this helmet in the wind tunnel. Going off the features that have been implemented, these are designed methodologies that have been used across a broad array of different aero helmets that have tested well.

Featuring large vents at the front combined with deep channels internally towards the exhausts has tended to reduce the pressure drag off the back of the rider’s helmet. Another feature that tends to work well is a fairly narrow profile, especially for riders who ride with their head in a more upright position, as it reduces the frontal area. The shape of the helmet and the venting is also similar to the Trek Ballista, with the rear vents positioned in a way that should help direct airflow over the back when in a more aggressive position.

Certainly, the performance of the helmet has not slowed down the professional riders who have been using it, but that is not a very good judge of performance given that Pogačar could probably be in a commuter helmet and still win.

The helmet has been designed using MET’s in-house wind tunnel, The Tube. Personally, I have no reason to doubt that the helmet is a strong performer. But as we have seen in our own testing, the performance of the helmet will likely vary compared to others based on the position of the rider using it.

For a more subjective measurement, the helmet is impressively light. It’s not as light as the POC Cytal Lite, but it does compare very favourably to many other aero helmets. For those wanting to reduce total system weight by as much as possible while maintaining aerodynamic performance, this helmet is a very strong contender.

I have also been using it for very long days in the saddle, and it’s been exceptionally comfortable. The padding is well distributed throughout, and the straps have a good range of adjustment.

The rear cradle adjustment is also very welcome, and the dial is easy to use. There are vents at the side that are designed to be able to house glasses when not wearing them; however, I found that not many glasses worked with these helmets.

Quite often the arm was a bit too thick and wouldn’t lodge into them. Scicon glasses, coincidentally used alongside MET by sponsored WorldTour teams, do fit well because they have very slim arms. POC, Oakley, and AlbaOptics fitted less well.

Unfortunately, with all these new aero features, reduced weight, and increased ventilation, the price of the helmet has now jumped up.

The previous helmet was £229.99 at RRP, often dipping into the £150 region online; the new helmet starts at £299.99 / $375 and places it in the same ballpark as the Giro Eclipse Pro, Specialized Evade 4, Fizik Kudo, Oakley Velo Mach, Sweet Protection Tucker III 2Vi and Ekoi R-Aero.

There are of course cheaper offerings, with the Trek Ballista and HJC Furion 3 being closer to the £200 /$250 bracket, while the Van Rysel RCR-F helmet remains a relative outlier at £129.99. But that shouldn’t be an outlier, and hopefully pressure brands to stop pushing prices higher and higher. Yes, wind tunnel testing and development is not cheap, but the RCR-F is a strong aero performer, so we know good aero helmets can be made and sold for less.

Compared to the competition, until we test the Manta 3 in the tunnel, we can’t categorically say how it compares. I can say from my own testing that ventilation is better than the Sweet Protection, and at speed, better than the Giro.

However, the Giro brow padding prevents sweat from getting into my eyes. The MET, though, is lighter. It really balances out somewhat evenly between the MET and the Giro for me, but I lean towards the Giro in warmer weather for the brow padding and white colour, while I lean towards the MET in cooler conditions and when speed is the focus.

If I were buying on a budget, I would still go for the Van Rysel and recommend that helmet to anyone who wants the best value-for-money aero helmet.

The MET Menta 3 is a full revolution of the previous Manta, while adding some fantastic features from the featherweight, airy Trenta Gen 2.

The new helmet is lighter, far better ventilated, and promises to be more aerodynamic as well. I can’t categorically comment on that last one, but many of the designed features implemented suggest it is a faster helmet for racing speeds.

It still relies on high speeds and more airflow for peak ventilation, so low-speed climbing can get more stuffy. While the glasses docking is not the best, it is also not necessary.

It does, however, cost a lot; I would have liked to see the inclusion of the gel padding, as well as a rear light as standard, to help justify a price hike of nearly 30% over the previous version.

I personally love the sleek look of the helmet, with the absolute white colourway looking great as well as this matte black, but gloss is better for avoiding marks. Drops one point for average glasses docking, but that isn’t weighted heavily as it renders an aero helmet not very aero so you shouldn’t do it.

I would prefer a gel padding that avoids sweat dripping in the eyes as with Giro helmets, and that option may be available but not as standard with the MET. Otherwise the helmet fits very well and works well with many different glasses.

At speed, the helmet is downright airy and in winter weather it’s been very cool. However, at low speeds and high effort, it can get warm, but so does virtually every good aero helmet. The black colour also heats up in direct sunlight, so white is a smarter choice.

Heavily crash tested, latest MIPS tech, good retention system, and a 5/5 VTH rating mean there is nothing I can criticise here.

We haven’t tested the helmet yet, but there is likely a good reason sponsored teams almost ditched the Trenta to race exclusively in the new Manta even in hot weather, so important is the aero advantage. It uses many tried and tested features and technologies that should ensure solid aero performance.

£300 is not cheap, but annoyingly is becoming something of the norm for top of the range aero road helmets. If it came with the gel padding and rear light as standard, it would score better, at present it is only beaten in price by a small handful of £300+ helmets, but sits in the same region as the Giro, Oakley, and Specialized competitors.

items.title: Yankees 2026 Roster Report Cards: Max Fried
items.author: John Griffin
items.content:
When Max Fried signed an eight-year, $218 million contract during the 2024-2025 offseason, the scouting report said that the Yankees were getting one of the game’s premier southpaws with impeccable defense, but who had regularly battled injuries throughout his career. Now at the contract’s quarter pole, that scouting report has played out as advertised. Across his first two years in pinstripes, Fried’s 8.3 fWAR and 2.83 ERA rank eighth and fifth, respectively, among starters with at least 300 innings pitched, and he took home the 2025 AL Gold Glove. After a mostly healthy 2025 that saw him throw a career-high 195 innings, however, the 32-year-old battled injuries this season, culminating in an offseason elbow surgery announced earlier this week.

20 starts, 112.2 IP, 2.80 ERA (150 ERA+), 2.65 FIP, 3.59 xFIP, 24.0 K%, 7.6 BB%, 3.5 fWAR, 3.7 rWAR

Entering third year of eight-year, $218 million contract

With Ace of the Past Gerrit Cole still rehabbing from Tommy John surgery and Ace of the Future Cam Schlittler about to explode on the scene, Fried was tabbed as the Yankees’ Opening Day starter in San Francisco — his fourth career Opening Day start, and first in pinstripes. He was characteristically dominant in that first start, allowing just two runs in 6.1 scoreless frames to set the tone not just for his 2026 performance, but that of the Yankees’ rotation as a whole.

When healthy this season, Fried was the definition of consistency. Across his 20 regular season starts, he allowed more than three runs just three times. One came against the LA Angels on April 16th, during that strange four-game set in the Bronx where the Yankees’ pitching staff randomly crumbled to pieces (they gave up 32 total runs against the American League’s second-worst offense). The second came on May 8th, where the future World Series champion Milwaukee Brewers put together a four-run second inning courtesy of four singles and a pair of walks; since he would hit the injured list with an elbow bruise following his next start, it’s fair to wonder whether he was beginning to feel the effects of the injury here. The third, and final, came in the final week of the season, as the Rays offense broke through in the seventh as he was outdueled by Tampa Bay ace Drew Rasmussen. Even in these three starts, however, Fried managed to give the Yankees length, going 5.1, 6, and 6.1 innings in each, respectively.

In his other 17 outings, Fried was magnificent. He surrendered one run or fewer in 12 of those outings, and struck out six or more nine times. More importantly, he continued to be elite at generating soft contact, ranking in the 99th percentile in barrel percentage, 97th percentile in hard hit percentage, 96th percentile in average exit velocity, and 83rd percentile in ground ball percentage.

Furthermore, when the lights shone brightest, Fried came up big. Taking the ball against Boston in Game 2 of the Wild Card Round, he spun six innings of one-run ball, striking out six and walking just one; the only blemish came on a Willson Contreras home run with two outs in the sixth, a wall-scraper that was Boston’s first postseason run since the sixth inning of Game 2 of the previous year’s Wild Card Round. He wasn’t quite as strong a week later, getting tagged with the loss as the Yankees got swept, but honestly, he pitched well enough to keep the Yankees in the ballgame: in truth, he really only made two bad pitches all night, although both unfortunately ended up in the seats.

As we look ahead to next season, there is a concern on the horizon: Fried’s injury history. As we know, elbows are a ticking time bomb for pitchers, even those like Fried who rely less on swing-and-miss stuff and more on soft contact. Even though Fried is on track to be a full go for the hypothetical spring training that starts on time, and will almost certainly be ready for whenever the teams actually report, we’re still going to want to keep an eye on his elbow going forward. That’s true for all pitchers, though, and at least with Fried, we know that, when he’s on the mound, he’s going to be an ace.

items.title: 'The most tradable sport nobody trades': Inside race prediction platform RPM
items.author: The Race Media
items.content:
RPM is the world’s first motorsport prediction platform, where every outcome of a race event becomes a tradable market. Fans are able to buy and sell outcomes on every moment of a race at a moment’s notice.

Founder Ben Jarrett joined The Race Business as part of our Spotlight series of interviews to explain how he spotted a niche in the motorsport market - and how RPM itself could play a part in changing how fans consume motorsport.

“RPM is at the intersection of motorsport, content creation, and prediction markets,” says Jarrett.

Will it rain? Who pits first? Which tyres do they choose?

Fans can essentially make predictions about every single facet of motorsport. And it’s an idea that was born out of a racetrack.

“I was racing GT4 cars, and I’m standing on the pitwall. Someone comes up and says: ‘10 bucks, he puts it into the wall at Turn 1’.

“The other guy’s like, ‘No, no, 100 bucks, he puts it [into the wall]’.

“Everyone was standing there. I was in my suit, I had my hands on my helmet, and we were supposed to go out there for practice before qualifying and put a lap in.”

It was at that moment that Jarrett had the idea to open up motorsport prediction markets to fans and content creators.

“I handed in my HANS device and my helmet to my mate and I drove home.”

He says the RPM app is as “simple as having a question that you want a large fanbase to help you solve. That’s a market: Max Verstappen to win in Australia, George Russell to make a pass for the lead on lap 10, or whenever”.

Jarrett says he’s found a gap in the market as motorsport fans don’t traditionally engage in iGaming - wagering on outcomes online - as other sports fans do, with football and basketball being the most popular sports in this regard.

“I would say there are 1.3 billion fans of motorsport. But in terms of iGaming volume, it provides less than half a percent.

“So, it's one of the most tradable sports on earth that nobody trades, that nobody touches.

“There are 72 days a year that F1 is on, and it’s becoming a part of people’s daily life.”

He points us to F1’s Global Fan Survey that, in 2025, found that 61% of motorsport fans engage with F1 content on a daily basis.

“So, this is a fan ecosystem that really is becoming part of people's daily life. And if we go and we look at social media… motorsport content is everywhere.”

RPM is also geared towards giving content creators their own space. Creators can build a standalone competition around an event - or keep the competition running all season with a running leaderboard - while RPM handles the predictions, scoring, credits, prizing support and league access.

Approved creators can even unlock revenue share opportunities with RPM in the future.

“I'm very interested in the content creators. And we use that word a lot because that's where we really see the opportunity. We want to give them a voice. We want to give them participation.

“We don't just see them as like a marketing push. We really see them as part of the heartbeat of what is RPM. This is a platform for them to come in, engage in motorsport on a daily basis, through markets, in a different way.”

items.title: Mathieu van der Poel's coach and father still in the dark over cyclo-cross participation this winter
items.author: Patrick Fletcher
items.content:
There is still a sense of mystery surrounding Mathieu van der Poel's cyclo-cross season, with the Dutch national coach saying he still doesn't know whether the star man will compete this winter and that Van der Poel's father doesn't, either.

Van der Poel has been a dominant force in cyclo-cross over the course of his career, winning eight world titles, but he has not yet committed to returning to the discipline this winter.

He is due to become a father in January, which is clearly a factor, and while he has not yet ruled out racing, he has not confirmed any plans so far, with the World Cup series starting in two weeks' time.

"I’m curious too," Van der Poel's national coach for cyclo-cross and mountain bike, Gerben de Knegt said this week on the Live Slow Ride Fast podcast of fellow Dutchmen Laurens ten Dam and Stefan Bolt.

"I’ve even asked [Van der Poel's father] Adrie about it, but he doesn’t know either."

Bolt, seeing the funny side, then chimed in: "Adrie is just as in the dark as the rest of us. It’s quite funny, really. People interview Adrie as if he has some special insight into Mathieu’s life."

De Knegt also highlighted Van der Poel's impending fatherhood, which is set to come in the middle of the season, in the same month as the World Championships, which take place right at the end of January.

"Of course, there’s the family aspect, when it comes to the idea of not doing any 'cross this winter. Well, given that he’s going to be a dad around January, this is actually the ideal winter to skip it," De Knegt said.

As for the possibility of dropping in just for the World Championships, he said: "I’ve discussed that with him often in the past. But it's not really an option. We’ve always preferred to do more races."

Van der Poel himself has hinted in the past that he could skip cyclo-cross entirely one winter.

After collecting his eighth world title in February earlier this year, he said: "Maybe it's not a bad idea to skip one winter because to be here it's the first peak of my season always, not only physically, but also mentally.

"This is a day when I want to be in top shape, 90% is not enough or would not be enough for me to be at the start line here."

items.title: Our verdict on Lawson earning a 2027 F1 extension
items.author: Jon Noble
items.content:
Liam Lawson and Arvid Lindblad will continue to race for Racing Bulls in 2027, with Red Bull electing against what would have been a huge Formula 1 driver sacking.

Here's what our team makes of the move to keep Lawson and Lindblad and not promote Formula 2 title contender Nikola Tsolov into a race seat.

An existential question has been answered

Very few driver decisions have felt as right as Lawson getting a fresh contract with Racing Bulls.

He has been superb this year. Yes, there are still some rough edges to smooth out, but he has been fast throughout, consistently strong, delivering technical input that his engineers have loved, and brilliantly able to shut out all the noise regarding the doubts over his future.

But there is a wider significance to Lawson getting a stay, and it's one I mentioned in Monday's From the Paddock newsletter. The Lawson decision was almost existential for Racing Bulls in telling us what that team is really about.

Sign up to our newsletter to be in with a chance of winning a signed Valtteri Bottas Cadillac F1 cap.

Is it an outfit that, under Alan Permane, can stand on its own two feet, take its own decisions and plot a path that is only focused on making itself better?

Or is it simply a puppet for sister squad Red Bull, a testing ground and training school for its future drivers, even if that means some short-term pain in rushing rookies through?

After the season Lawson has had, it would have made no sense for Racing Bulls to drop him and throw away all the good momentum it has built up. So keeping him for now gives us the answer about what Racing Bulls is about.

Tsolov has a bright future in F1, but time is on his side to make that step up.

The best decision for all involved

Pretty sure this is the best decision for Racing Bulls and in the future for Red Bull.

Both Lawson and Lindblad - a rookie, let's not forget - have shown that they can bring home the results when everything goes as planned over a race weekend.

Both are capable of being a replacement for Isack Hadjar or Max Verstappen if either of them slip on a banana skin. Red Bull knows what Lawson can bring to them if required, so he is a good measure of what Lindblad could potentially bring too.

Having Tsolov in the background and doing a few FP1 sessions will prepare him for an introduction in 2028.

As far as I'm concerned, it's the correct decision for all involved. 

Credibility for Racing Bulls

If Racing Bulls is to be at all seen as an F1 team in its own right, with its own ambitions and dreams and what have you, rather than a pure Red Bull talent farm, then yeah, Lawson pretty much had to be kept on.

Tsolov may end up faster down the line. For all we know, he may be faster already. But the kind of efficient scoring that Lawson has provided this year a rookie cannot match - I would say that's a rule in F1.

So Tsolov-for-Lawson would be nakedly sacrificing Racing Bulls's present for the senior Red Bull team's future, and every decision like that makes it less and less palatable for Red Bull to own two teams in F1.

Only if Racing Bulls has its own aspirations can it be allowed to continue, and a new deal for Lawson buys some credibility in my eyes.

Marko would have dropped Lawson long ago

At the height of his powers, Helmut Marko would have ditched Lawson ages ago.

Lawson had his shot at the top team, didn't make it, and will likely not be given that chance again.

Now Marko's no longer in charge, and this is the biggest indicator yet that Racing Bulls is not Toro Rosso; developing young drivers is no longer the only, or primary, end goal for this team.

You can't blame Red Bull. Instead of a team that cost and lost money to run like Toro Rosso, Racing Bulls is now a multi-billion dollar entity. Constructors' championship finishing position is not the only definition of value in an F1 business anymore.

Taking risks with a team built with the acceptance of losing money is one thing. Taking risks with a team worth billions is another.

None of this is to criticise the decision it has made, as Lawson is a worthy F1 driver. It's just to point out yet more evidence that Racing Bulls is acting and being run like its own team.

Lawson would be wise to find an exit route

Lawson is in a fantastic position now and has been one of the star drivers of the season, but he should already be thinking about exit routes for 2028.

Tsolov is going to be waiting in the wings next year, and there's no reason why Racing Bulls might be faced with the exact same 'three into two' dilemma for 2028.

This time Lawson was the overwhelmingly logical pick, next time he might not be and, given Red Bull leaves those decisions until late in the season, he doesn't want to suddenly be left without a seat for 2028.

So he'd be wise to try to follow the Pierre Gasly and Carlos Sainz playbook of finding another driver Red Bull decides it's done with you.

Adds to an excellent redemption arc

I've got a lot of time for this career redemption arc.

Lawson at the Red Bull senior team always felt like an uncomfortable fit to me, right from when it was announced. I certainly hadn't seen anything to suggest he would solve the team's second-driver problem.

Red Bull's bungling of what followed didn't help, but that ill-fated, two-race spell could've marked the beginning of the end of Lawson's F1 career.

Instead, what's followed has revealed plenty about his mental resolve - because he's had to process a lot these past 20 months yet has been absolutely unflappable. 

Driving for the top teams is what every driver craves, but it doesn't have to be the be-all and end-all and, if you don't make it, it doesn't automatically consign you to career collapse.

Lawson's proved emphatically this year that he deserves a place in F1. This contract extension was therefore the only acceptable outcome.

items.title: Cavaliers 115, Knicks 107: “Credit them, but…”
items.author: Moritz Wollert
items.content:
As sports fans, our teams give us plenty to think about and then some. They give us stuff to bicker, to complain, to ramble about. We follow their every move meticulously, we break down the potential of prospective grocery baggers and hail them as the next coming. We love to read or listen to others doing the same, even or especially if we do not agree with their viewpoints. Lucky fanatics get something to cheer about every once in a while – consider that box checked by our beloved New York Knickerbockers lately.

Understandably, that focus on one team, that love for one franchise can lead to kind of a narrow view on things at times. Nothing wrong with that; fandom doesn’t have to be rational, it doesn’t have to explain itself. And it does not necessarily have to involve the other team’s perspective or, frankly, the other team at all. At times though, that group in the different colored jerseys is the biggest answer to the question you have regarding your own squad’s performance.

Last night felt exactly like that kind of game where the Knicks did a lot of stuff well, but in the end the Cleveland Cavaliers just did most of it a little bit better. And when the Knicks didn’t do something as well, it was also the Cavaliers who had a hand in that. From the opening tip, it was obvious that the Cavs wanted this one – analytically and this time around actually in reality, too. They remembered last Saturday when New York rained on their Rocket Arena parade on the second night of a back-to-back; they surely remembered the last time they visited Madison Square Garden. And it looked like they were tired of the narrative that had them as the soft wannabes that can’t keep up when the orange and blue drivers push the pedals to the metal.

Cavaliers put an end to Knicks’ winning streak

Donovan Mitchell lived in the lane for most of the night; every high slip screen was an automatic downhill and kick opportunity for the team from Ohio, and their old and new length bothered the smaller Knicks for long stretches of the game. Peyton Watson might not be able to hit the water from the Verrazzano Bridge right now, but he sure can impact a game defensively. A lot of the Ohioans were feeling good about themselves; Tyrese Proctor and Meleek Thomas gave youthful, quality energy off the bench. And then, of course, there was James Harden. That guy who is a poster child for a lot of ugly wrongs in the modern game, the one who has been awful all year long so far but decided to show up for this one and give his team a vintage performance in the very building he crapped the postseason bed in just half a year ago.

So even if, at least in Harden’s case, it’s hard to stomach, let’s follow Knicks Fan in Jerusalem’s proposal from the Postgame Thread that gave this text its headline. Let’s credit the Cavaliers for a game well played, for shots hit, for storms weathered. But as the headline and our friend in Israel suggested, there’s another side to the story, a “but”. Tipping our collective cap to the Cavs sure doesn’t mean the Knicks can’t do a lot of things better in the future. Jalen Brunson had a good scoring game yet failed to deliver any rhythm to the offense. Too many times the ball just stuck on the perimeter (a particular problem for OG Anunoby right now), and there wasn’t nearly enough off-ball movement to stretch a much bigger defense that wants you to finish over their size.

That size played quite a role in yesterday’s contest, be it on the boards or in the passing lanes. Unfortunately, the Knicks won’t get any taller, that’s for sure. Mike Brown tried to counter Cleveland’s length by going to Mohamed Diawara early in the absence of Jordan Clarkson. Mo had a nice drive and, in theory, could be a solution for physical matchup problems like this one, but clearly isn’t there yet. The young Frenchman seems unsure about himself, plays hesitantly, and is missing the wide-open shots he knocked down in his sleep last season. His defense mostly looks good but not good enough to warrant a bigger role yet.

So, what’s happening with Mikal Bridges?

Aside from plenty of mental lapses, missing open shots was a problem for Josh Hart last night as well, but we excuse the veteran as he clearly had to shake off some rust after his injury break. That doesn’t change the fact that his lack of consistent outside shooting can become an issue at times, especially against good teams that willingly put roaming defenders on him. Normally, he adds so many other intangibles that you can live with it in the bigger picture more often than not. In Mikal Bridges’ case, though, well, what’s there right now? Hounding defense? Don’t see it consistently. A presence off the ball? Nope. Secondary scoring? Corner threes? Emotion? Desperation? Anything?

Bridges once again played an uneventful, meager 17 minutes in this one. Plenty of the other guards – Deuce McBride, Landry Shamet, and Tyler Kolek – currently do everything Bridges is paid for and actually a bit more. The longer this situation drags on, the louder Mike Brown will hear the question: When will you make a change to the starting lineup? It’s easy to understand why he’s reluctant; he sure doesn’t want to create an internal problem by benching someone who did his part in winning a championship last year. But what if the problem is creating itself? There’s a tipping point to everything.

For the Knicks, this game won’t be one, and it shouldn’t be. There might be some stuff to think about, though, going forward. Just like we want to have it as fans.

items.title: Denmark announced as host of 2027 UEC Road European Championships
items.author: cyclingnews@futurenet.com (Dani Ostanek)
items.content:
It's the first time the nation has hosted a major road championship since the 2017 European Championships, also held in Herning, when Alexander Kristoff and Marianne Vos raced to glory in the road races while Victor Campenaerts and Ellen van Dijk won the time trials.

Previously, the Road World Championships were held in Copenhagen, Denmark, in 2011, while the Road Worlds will head back to the nation in 2029.

Previous major championships held in Denmark have ended with mass sprint finishes, and the 2027 European Championships are also expected to favour sprinters after hilly editions in Slovenia and France in the last two years.

The 2027 UEC Road European Championships will run between September 28 and October 3, and while the exact dates of each event are not yet known, that creates a clash with La Vuelta Femenina, which begins on October 3.

"We are thrilled to be returning to Denmark after ten years. In 2017, this country hosted the second edition of the Road European Championships open to the Elite category, believing from the outset in a project that was then in its infancy," said UEC president Enrico Della Casa.

"Today, we are returning with an event that has grown considerably and has become a world-class occasion, capable of attracting the attention of the media and cycling enthusiasts from all over the world."

Hosting of the European Championships is now set for the next three years, with trips to Denmark, the North Brabant region of the Netherlands, and Abruzzo in Italy on the way.

"With Denmark in 2027, the Netherlands in 2028 and Italy, specifically the Abruzzo region, in 2029, the next three years promise to be highly prestigious for the UEC Road European Championships. These three countries, each with a deeply rooted cycling culture, demonstrate the appeal our event has gained and allow us to look to the future with great ambition," said Della Casa.

"I would like to thank the cities of Herning and Silkeborg, Sport Event Denmark, the Danish government and the Danish Cycling Federation and its President, Morten Anderson, for the trust, enthusiasm and commitment they have shown.

"Ten years ago, Denmark helped to write an important chapter in the history of our European Championships, and I am convinced that in 2027, together we will write another equally memorable one."

items.title: Red Bull's Lawson decision is a clean break from its Marko era
items.author: Edd Straw
items.content:
Lawson’s seat in Red Bull’s second team has been at very real risk in recent rounds, with Formula 2 race winner Nikola Tsolov waiting in the wings and Red Bull needing to decide which two of Lawson, Tsolov and Arvid Lindblad race for Racing Bulls next year. 

But had Lawson lost out - with zero options elsewhere on the grid to race in 2027 - it would have been an unprecedented move.

In the past 10 seasons of F1, there have only been two comparable cases of a driver doing as well as Lawson is currently doing, getting dropped and then not having an alternative seat for the following season.

Only Sergio Perez - who was eighth in the 2024 championship - and Alex Albon - who was seventh in the 2020 championship - have been higher placed than Lawson is right now (ninth) and yet found themselves without a drive the year after.

Both, of course, met that fate thanks to Red Bull, but the big difference is both Perez and Albon were driving for Red Bull Racing - and getting absolutely destroyed by Max Verstappen in the process.

Lawson is in a completely different situation here, in that he’s the highest-placed of all midfield drivers in the 2026 world championship and comfortably ahead of his rookie team-mate Lindblad.

The main threat to Lawson’s position comes from F2 title contender Tsolov. The Bulgarian has won six races in his rookie F2 season and sits only seven points behind 2027 Haas F1 driver and Ferrari junior Rafael Camara - who made his F1 debut in place of Esteban Ocon in Brazil.

Tsolov has made a strong case for promotion, not only because of those F2 results but also because of how well he did subbing for Lawson in a mandated rookie FP1 outing in Mexico, where Tsolov lapped within two tenths of Lindblad and generally looked very at ease with the whole business of being in F1.

On top of Tsolov’s impressive showing in Mexico, Lawson later had a run-in with Red Bull’s kingpin driver Verstappen during FP2 - which earned Lawson a strong rebuke from the four-time champion, in which Verstappen alluded to Lawson’s 2027 deal uncertainty.

The Race understands the recent triple-header has basically been the crunch moment for Red Bull and Racing Bulls to do their final analysis on who should drive next year - so Lawson been under pressure during this period and at genuine risk of losing his seat.

Which perhaps explains Verstappen’s pointed remark in the wake of their collision in Mexico, “It’s just not very smart behaviour when you’re in his position to pick a fight with me.”

But the way Lawson rebounded from that low point, recovering from a technical exclusion in qualifying and a pitlane start to finish seventh that weekend, in his familiar position as the leading midfield runner, showed true grit.

Add that to the way Lawson excelled in the wet in Brazil - fifth in qualifying and seventh in the race - and it’s difficult for anyone inside the Red Bull system to make the case he should definitely be dropped.

It has only been Lawson at real risk - because Lindblad has done an excellent job alongside him as a rookie and contributed a meaningful 35% of the points that leave Racing Bulls almost certain to finish fifth in the constructors’ championship - the highest place in the team’s history.

Lawson’s job within that team is essentially to give Red Bull a benchmark of performance to measure Lindblad against. There’s no realistic possibility of Lawson becoming a contender for a Red Bull Racing seat again, in the way there might still be for Lindblad or, eventually, Tsolov.

The trouble is that Lawson has done such an excellent job in his role this season - and has even taken a further step as a driver since subbing for Isack Hadjar at Red Bull for three races - that he made himself impossible to drop even though his presence no longer really fits the 'Red Bull conveyor belt' function Racing Bulls is supposed to have.

On Friday in Brazil, Racing Bulls team boss Alan Permane said Racing Bulls is trying to “apply a little bit of science” to the situation, a clear rebuke of the days when Helmut Marko would hire and fire junior drivers seemingly almost on a whim. 

“Red Bull's had a very successful young driver programme, and if I want to be... and I don't want to be critical of it, but I think if you guys are critical of it, maybe sometimes the drivers haven't been able to have enough time to settle, or maybe some snap decisions have been made,” Permane said.

Lawson’s average qualifying advantage over Lindblad is only seven hundredths of a second, but in the races - where the points are paid out - Lawson has a clear advantage.

He’s scored in 13 of the 17 grands prix he’s started for Racing Bulls this year, as well as taking points in three of the six sprint races staged. He’s also finished ahead of Lindblad 11 times out of the 14 races they have both finished and run ahead of him on 77% of the racing laps both completed.

That’s made him the undisputed king of the midfield. Of the 52 qualifying sessions and races, including sprints, held this year, Lawson has been classified at the top of that group 18 times.

To put that number in context, remember Alpine and Audi have made the fight at the front of that group a close one, and that Lawson wasn’t part of the midfield for eight of those because he was in Hadjar’s Red Bull.

His approach has also caught the eye. Prior to 2026, there were times when his decision-making in battle could be self-defeating. That led to more on-track incidents than necessary.

That’s something he’s largely cut out this year, while still fighting hard enough to get the results.

He’s also adapted well to the 2026 cars, recognising he needed to contain the desire to over-drive to get the most out of them - not easy to do for a driver who can be naturally aggressive on corner entries.

He’s also able to piece together weekends consistently well, often turning things round even if they start badly on Friday.He also did a good job in those three outings for Red Bull, despite the scars of what happened to him in 2025. That shows a mental robustness, which is also reflected in his mindset amid uncertainty about his future. He’s been able to focus on doing his job and not been distracted by this - something that is easier said than done.

Lawson explained: “A year ago I thought about it a lot. It was very much in my head and you just drive worse when you overthink things.”

Lawson hasn’t suddenly transformed himself into the best driver in F1. But he’s taken a big step to become a rounded, consistent, and dependable midfield performer - and a very quick one too.

That’s what eventually made him undroppable for 2027. 

Permane had already suggested “everyone will be happy” when the announcement finally came, so that suggests that now Lawson has been confirmed alternative arrangements will be made for Tsolov - which will most likely mean an official reserve driver role and an expanded programme of F1 testing and free practice running in 2027.

items.title: Racing Bulls officially keeps Lawson for 2027
items.author: Jon Noble
items.content:
Liam Lawson will remain at Racing Bulls next season after the squad announced an unchanged Formula 1 line-up for 2027.

The New Zealander’s future had been uncertain for many weeks, with the Red Bull-owned outfit pondering whether to keep him on alongside Arvid Lindblad or promote its junior driver Nikola Tsolov.

However, as reported earlier this week, Lawson’s recent strong performances in Mexico and Brazil were understood to have put him on course for a new deal and convinced Racing Bulls he was the best candidate.

With Lawson currently sitting ninth in the drivers’ standings, as best of the rest behind the top four teams, and his contribution key to helping Racing Bulls sit fifth in the constructors’ championship, it would have been nonsensical to have dropped him.

Racing Bulls team principal Alan Permane believed that the line-up of Lawson and Lindblad was the perfect one in terms of blending youth and experience.

“Both have demonstrated their ability and potential throughout the season, and we’ve seen the progress they’ve made, both individually and as a pairing,” explained Permane.

“I have no doubt that this is the best driver line-up for us, bringing a strong combination of experience and ambition. Together, we have a solid foundation to build on the progress made this year, continue pushing ourselves forward and take the next step towards achieving our ambitions in 2027."

Lawson has earned praise in the paddock this year for his standout performances for both Racing Bulls and during a stand-in run at Red Bull, when he filled in for the injured Isack Hadjar.

He thanked Racing Bulls for the belief in him.

“We've had a brilliant season together and the team has worked very hard to produce a fast car, which I've loved driving,” he said.

“It feels great to be part of a historic season for the team as we continue our fight for P5 in the constructors' championship.

"It's a testament to the hard work of everyone both at track, and back at the factory. I’m looking forward to carrying this momentum forward with Arvid through to 2027; we're building something super positive and I’m excited by what we can achieve together.”

The Racing Bulls statement that announced Lawson and Lindblad were staying for 2027 did not make any reference to plans for Tsolov, who is in the hunt to clinch the F2 crown this year.

The Bulgarian had a rookie FP1 run for Racing Bulls in Mexico, and will likely have a wider role with Red Bull in 2027. He has also been linked with a switch to Super Formula in Japan.

items.title: 'No serious damage' – Lucinda Brand escapes serious injury following her crash at the Niel Superprestige
items.author: Owen Rogers
items.content:
After initially fearing the worst, Lucinda Brand was not seriously injured when she hit the barrier during the Superprestige Jaarmarktcross cyclo-cross race at Niel on Wednesday.

Early on during round three of the season-long Superprestige series, World Champion Brand briefly lost control of her bike, hitting the barrier and twisting her ankle as she put her foot down.

Despite what was apparently an innocuous incident, her discomfort was clear immediately; the 37-year-old first grimaced, then fell into tears, before abandoning the race she had hoped to win for a fifth time.

After the incident, her Baloise Verzekeringen-Het Poetsbureau Lions team manager, former World Champion Sven Nys, was fearful Brand had suffered a severe injury, telling Play Sport: "If Lucinda has tears in her eyes, that is usually not a good sign. She is quite a tough cookie, which is why I am a bit worried now."

Then, in a post on the team’s Instagram account, he added: "She can’t put force on her foot right now, so I think it’s important that we monitor that and make sure that nothing was damaged.

"Hoping we won’t lose her for the rest of the season."

However, Nys has since been reassured. "Everything is okay. No serious damage was detected; she just needs to make sure it doesn’t happen again. Taping the foot is important now, though," he told Belgian paper .

The season continues apace this weekend, and Brand would have been expected to start round four of the Superprestige at Merkplas on Saturday and Sunday’s Bollekesccross, the second round of the X2O Badkamers Trofee, a series she leads, after winning the Koppenbergcross, and which she has won on four previous occasions. However, following her injury, Brand’s participation is yet to be confirmed.

items.title: 'I don't get often very emotional' – Tadej Pogačar highlights a teammate's Tour de France stage win as 'one of the best days of my career'
items.author: Patrick Fletcher
items.content:
Tadej Pogačar has no shortage of highlights from his eight years so far as a professional bike racer but he has picked out a teammate’s victory as "one of the best days of my career".

"The first stages, nine, was really nice," Pogačar says from a massage table, presumably after stage nine as he talks about it being “super hot” and references "three victories" taken by the team.

"I think the one that Isaac wins, in Barcelona, I got also really emotional, and I don’t get often very emotional," Pogačar says.

"So, one of the best days of my career," he adds.

The comments are brief but striking in the context of all that Pogačar has won, including five Tour de France titles, 26 Tour de France stages of his own, 13 Monument Classics, and two world titles.

For all the talk of his insatiable appetite for victory, he seemingly took just as much joy in sacrificing the chance of another one and helping someone else, who may one day come to rival him.

And it wasn’t just that day in Barcelona; with a commanding lead in the yellow jersey Pogačar went on to effectively work as a domestique for Del Toro again and again in the second half of the Tour de France, notably on the stage 15 summit finish at Plateau de Solaison and on the penultimate day to Alpe d’Huez when Del Toro’s podium position came under fire from Paul Seixas.

"You try to be the best version of yourself but we don’t know how we are perceived in the third person," Del Toro said in a recent interview with Spanish newspaper in reference to Pogačar’s treatment of him.

"That he can see something that maybe I’m not seeing is flattering, but also quite something. He wants to be part of my process and support me in each opportunity. It’s something very beautiful and I feel very privileged."
