Russell launches fully-funded new karting academy
items.author: Fleur Mealing
items.content:
Mercedes Formula 1 driver George Russell has launched a new karting academy at Silverstone aimed at developing the next generation of motorsport talent, with 25 young drivers set to receive a fully funded championship opportunity in 2027.

The GR63 Karting Academy will be open to boys and girls aged eight and nine, with Russell hoping to provide a route into motorsport for talented youngsters who might otherwise be held back by the financial demands of the sport.

Based at Silverstone's karting circuit, the initiative will run across four stages, beginning with open-access qualifying sessions in December 2026.

The first stage will see eligible drivers compete in arrive-and-drive sessions between December 6 and 31, with the 80 fastest progressing to a shootout on January 31, 2027.

From there, 25 drivers will be selected for the GR63 Championship, an eight-round series running from March to November 2027. Each round will take place on a different circuit configuration at Silverstone, with all participation costs covered by the academy.

The 25 selected drivers will also receive a full set of academy equipment, including racing overalls, a helmet, gloves and boots.

The programme will culminate in December 2027, when the championship's top five finishers compete in a final race at Silverstone. Drivers will be evaluated on their talent, lap times, fitness, racecraft and media skills, with the overall winner receiving a fully-funded karting season in 2028.

Russell will help mentor and guide participants throughout the programme.

"Karting is where it all started for me, and it taught me everything I've relied on throughout my career," said Russell.

"I know how hard it is for talented young drivers to get that first opportunity, especially when budgets are tight.

"With the GR63 Karting Academy, I want to give something back by finding those hidden talents and giving them the support and platform they need to reach their potential."

The financial accessibility of the programme is a central part of its appeal. While the initial qualifying sessions will cost £25 and entry to the January shootout will cost £75, everything from the championship stage onwards will be fully funded.

The initiative is being supported by Silverstone and the British Racing Drivers' Club (BRDC), with BRDC president David Coulthard welcoming the opportunity to invest in Britain's motorsport future.

"The GR63 Academy captures that ethos perfectly, and we are delighted to work with George to support the next generation of drivers here at Silverstone," said Coulthard.

How to enter the GR63 Karting Academy

The initial arrive-and-drive qualifying sessions will take place at Silverstone Kart Track between December 6 and 31, 2026, at a cost of £25.

All applicants must be citizens of a Commonwealth country.

items.title: Why Mercedes cannot dominate F1's new era
items.author: Jon Noble
items.content:
They say history doesn't repeat itself, but it often rhymes. And that applies to Formula 1 as well.

The start of new-rules eras have often been hugely indicative of what is to come, as the trends of the inaugural season lay down the story of future years.

If we do some comparisons of the first years of the most recent major rules-change eras, we can see how the comparisons between the first and second half of each of those seasons gave us a hint of what was to come in the following campaigns.

Constructors' championship splits

Represented as first half / second half / total

: 112 / 60 / 172: 92.5 / 61.0 / 153.5: 14 / 57 / 71: 32 / 38 / 70: 34.5 / 25 / 59.5

: 366 / 335 / 701: 188 / 217 / 405: 121 / 199 / 320: 116 / 100 / 216: 96 / 85 / 181

2022 (22 rounds; 11 / 11)

: 359 / 400 / 759: 303 / 251 / 554: 237 / 278 / 515: 81 / 92 / 173: 81 / 78 / 159

2026 (23 rounds; 20 completed so far; 11 / 9)

: 379 / 273 / 652: 307 / 203 / 510: 177 / 238 / 415: 222 / 176 / 398

In 2009, Brawn GP took the crowns thanks to its stellar start to the year, but you could see Red Bull getting its act together ahead of what became its era of dominance.

In 2014, Mercedes was unstoppable and its advantage through the year clearly told us about it becoming the main force in F1.

In 2022, Ferrari started well but Red Bull got the weight off its car and pushed forward to begin Max Verstappen's real run of supremacy, off the back of his maiden title the year before.

For 2026, Mercedes has secured both crowns, but the story of the year is an intriguing one because a trend has emerged of there being no clear benchmark late on.

While Kimi Antonelli and George Russell kicked 2026 off strongly and laid title-winning foundations early on, subsequent spells of success for Red Bull, McLaren and Ferrari have pointed to a shift.

In fact, as the table below shows, if you take the results of the last five races up until and including Brazil, Mercedes is only the third-highest-scoring team.

Top four constructors (last five rounds)

Last five total points: 152Overall total: 415 (3rd0

Last five total points: 132Overall total: 510 (2nd)

Last five total points: 114Overall total: 652 (1st)

Last five total points: 92Overall total: 398 (4tth)

F1 has a super-close top four where no team seems to have been able to edge clear of its rivals, and it has been hard to pick out anyone who has built up some momentum.

This is why, for all the joy that Mercedes team principal Toto Wolff has taken from getting his team back to title-winning ways, he has no sense that this is the start of "runaway" success.

"It looks like the most competitive era that is about to start," he said.

"The teams have become so professional in capability and resource that these kind of runaway seasons, I don't see them anymore, whether it's four in a row or eight in a row. And that is a completely new challenge.

"You can see how quickly it goes from you being dominant and within a few races you realise that your upgrade doesn't work and you fall back and you're just third on the road. So it's great for the sport.

"I wish it was the era of Mercedes and me running away with another few championships. I don't think it's the reality."

The upgrade war seems to have had the effect of repeatedly shuffling the order of the top four.

Whenever any of the major teams have brought big development steps, often those have helped push them to the front and changed the hierarchy.

McLaren team principal Andrea Stella has labelled this "ping pong season" in terms of how teams bounce between being at the front or the back of that top-four block.

"Anybody that upgrades kind of takes an advantage, but even if you do a good job of developing, not necessarily [is it the case that] you can establish yourself at the top," he said recently.

"We have a variable level of supremacy, dependent on the track conditions or the optimisation of the set-up.

"But the reality is that I think nowhere before we have had F1 so competitive and with such a rate of development. If we raced with the race-one car [from the Australia season opener], we will be one and a half seconds slower than what we are at the moment."

The cause of this major shuffling is not only the fact that the big teams all seem to be so evenly matched in terms of their capability. (And have found ways to all keep pushing on with developments under the cost cap.)

It is that the FIA appears to have made life very difficult for teams because the aero regulations are so restrictive, leaving designers with only very small areas they can work on.

Focused on creating cars that did not produce significant dirty air, the FIA was determined not to allow areas that teams could exploit to ruin this and improve downforce.

And this has left teams capped in terms of how much performance they have been able to eke out.

Stella added: "If you take the regulations and you define the volumes within which you can put aerodynamic devices, that's not how an aerodynamicist would do it.

"They [the rules] have been done in a certain way somehow to jeopardise for the sake of competition and also for the sake of allowing the following and the overtaking."

Red Bull team principal Laurent Mekies agreed on the lack of design freedom leading to diminishing returns for all teams.

"The convergence is probably happening earlier than what we all thought," he said. "I'm guessing somehow, it's perhaps an indication of fairly restrictive regulations.

"That being said, you see cars with visibly different concepts and you see four top teams fighting, which is probably a great point to be for the sport.

"So, let's see how it will pan out in the second year. But to be already in the second part of '26 in situations where you turn up at the race weekend and you don't know which one of the four top teams is going to win the race, I think it's great for the sport."

The end result of all this is a form book that is in a state of flux.

Ferrari team principal Fred Vasseur thought that the 'ping pong' element of rapidly shuffling fortunes was a consequence of immature rules offering potential for big gains, something that will slow down into next season where he felt teams would converge more.

"Each time that we were bringing something, we are doing a step," he said. "That was a little bit the story of the season because, as we [the top-four teams] were not bringing upgrades at the same races, you have this kind of rotation.

"Probably it could be less through next year and the following years, but we will have a kind of convergence of performance of where we are next year."

And it's for this reason that Wolff was convinced that it is important Mercedes gets back to its early performance levels now that give it a springboard into next year.

"Look at the last few races: we haven't won [Mercedes has one win in the last five]," he said in Brazil.

"The competition has been getting tougher, between Ferrari, McLaren, Red Bull and ourselves. It's four teams that can win races and will be challenging for a world championship. And I have no doubt that it's going to be very difficult for us next year.

"For me, the 2027 season has started now."

items.title: Cavaliers 115, Knicks 107: Scenes from a wide free throw gap
items.author: Russell Richardson
items.content:
Four nights ago, in Cleveland, the Knicks beat the Cavaliers by 12 points thanks to dominant second and third quarters. Tonight, as we saluted our veterans, the two teams squared up once more, this time at Madison Square Garden. Yet again, our heroes dropped the first frame, but won the second, tied the third, and managed to tie the game midway through the fourth. The Cavs were determined not to let this one slip through their fingers, and with season-highs for two of ’em, James Harden (32 PTS, 9-14 FG) and Tyrese Proctor (15 PTS), they sealed the win in the final minutes, 115-107.

With his eleventh double-double, Karl-Anthony Towns (21 PTS, 11 RBS, 7-11 FG) tied Willis Reed for the longest double-double streak to start a Knicks season. They shot better from the floor and in the paint, but the guests attempted 14 more free throws. It didn’t help that New York surrendered 19 points off turnovers.

Last week, Peyton Watson (7 PTS) took most of Cleveland’s shots to start the game. This time, Kenny Atkinson’s club leveled its attack. Their defense hummed, too, with Evan Mobley (10 PTS, 5 RBS) and Watson swatting down shots, and Donovan Mitchell (23 PTS) and Harden picking pockets. Benchman Proctor led the team with eight points in the quarter, while Watson crashed the boards and spread out dimes. Jarrett Allen, who missed last week’s contest, cleared five early boards and finished with an 11-14 double-double.

Josh Hart (6 PTS, 26 MIN), back in the lineup after missing three games (ankle, illness), surely had nothing to do with the Knicks’ starters dragging their heels. Jalen Brunson (27 PTS, 12-23 FG) and OG Anunoby (14 PTS) were the only Knicks with points until Mohamed Diawara checked in midway through the frame and scored. Mitchell picked on the sophomore, dribbled around him, and burned him with a fadeaway.

The hometown club converted 25% of its first eight longball tries and attempted no free throws in the first frame. Strange but true. Towns, Brunson, and Shamet had the hot hands early, while Mikal Bridges, Josh Hart, and Andre Drummond combined to shoot 0-for-6 in the first half. Bridges would usually defend Mitchell, but Brown assigned Shamet to him. You can feel the coach’s confidence waning, no?

The Ohio Players hit nine straight shots, led by as many as 12, and won the quarter, 33–23.

We weren’t sweating the first quarter. New York dropped the first period by one in their previous matchup. Tonight, they opened the second on a 9–1 run behind Towns, Shamet, and Tyler Kolek. The latter hit two buckets and was a team-high plus-eight as the good guys climbed back into the game. Towns was cooking, too, scoring 13 points in his first 13 minutes, grabbing seven boards, and stuffing Allen’s shot. Miles McBride hit three threes in under two minutes, including the one that erased the last of a 12-point deficit and knotted the game at 43.

Brunson splashed a go-ahead three, but Harden answered with two of his own, Mitchell hit his freebies, and Mobley dunked to push Cleveland’s lead back to six. Mike Brown tried to give Towns a breather and watched the Knicks’ progress evaporate without him. KAT jumped back in and dunked with authority.

During the period, Brunson reached 11,000 career points, 3,000 assists, and 1,000 three-pointers. He’s one of seven active players in that club, along with LeBron James, Harden, Damian Lillard, Devin Booker, Luka Dončić, and Trae Young. Congratulations, Cap!

At halftime, the guests were ahead 59–53. Harden led all scorers with 17 (5-of-7 FG), while KAT topped the Knicks with 15. Bizarrely, New York took a single free throw all half, and Cleveland’s seven extra points at the line more than covered the margin. Both teams made 22 field goals (52% for Cleveland, 51% for New York) and grabbed 17 boards apiece. Cleveland had a 26–20 edge in the paint, but New York shot 40% from three to the Cavs’ 37% and scored one more point from the field.

Cleveland opened the third on a 10–5 run, with threes from Watson, Mitchell, and Harden stretching the lead to 69–58. Spida missed his next two threes and picked up a charge. From there, the hosts got serious. Brunson scored five of his eight points in the stretch during an 11–0 run that tied the tilt at 69, while the visitors blanked on eight consecutive attempts. Towns helped fuel the run by setting up Brunson and Shamet for buckets and blocking Watson at the cup. Hart later found McBride for another tying three at 74. Cleveland closed the quarter on an 8–2 run to take an 82–76 advantage into Q4.

Rough stretch for Bridges. He sat at the eight-minute mark of the third and came back with under two minutes left in the quarter. Allen blocked him on a layup, then took the ball away. Somehow, New York had attempted just five free throws through 40 minutes, all by Towns. The Cavs had taken 19 by then, eight by Harden alone.

Deuce scored the first five points of the fourth to pull the Knicks within one, but Mitchell answered with two layups, the second an and-one, and Proctor capped a 7–0 Cleveland run. Spida had two turnovers that led to McBride baskets, but he also set up Maleek Thomas for two buckets. With Brunson on the bench, McBride and Kolek ran the backcourt. Kolek fed Shamet for a three and KAT for a dunk that cut the deficit to seven with 7:35 left. Anunoby went on a tear with two freebies, a longball, a steal, and a breakaway feed to Hart for a bunny. Tie score at 99 with 5:36 to go.

Out of a timeout, Harden, Mobley, and Brunson scored to make it 106–103 with 2:18 on the clock. The game was still within reach, but Drummond fouled Mitchell and Allen scored four straight points, capitalizing on Brunson’s long brick. The deficit reached five with a minute to go. Brunson missed on a contested drive, Watson blocked McBride from behind on the fast break, and Harden hit his free throws. Ball game.

A Cup game in Indiana on Friday. Mo is tightening the bolts on his recap. Safe travels, Knickerbockers.

items.title: Game Discussion Thread: Knicks vs. Cavaliers, November 11, 2026
items.author: Russell Richardson
items.content:
The rising Knicks (6–4) host the falling Cleveland Cavaliers (5–6) tonight in New York City. They clashed last week in Cleveland, when the Knicks rode two dominant middle quarters to victory, despite late efforts by Donovan Mitchell. Hat’s off to Spida for averaging 22.8 points and 5.5 assists per game while carrying an old bearded man on his back. Mitchell must think he’s in a Samuel Beckett play. items.title: Classic British steel bike maker Temple Cycles set to close after 12 years in business
items.author: Owen Rogers
items.content:
Bristol-based bike maker Temple Cycles is set to close after more than 12 years in business, with its two shops also shutting down.

The company specialises in manufacturing steel-framed bikes, selling them either online or from its Bristol- and London-based shops, but will close down, with all its premises already listed as closed online.

However, the company’s website and social media accounts are still live, and though most models are listed as sold out, orders for frame sets, parts and accessories are invited in a Facebook post as recently as Tuesday, November 10.

That was the same day local news site, Bristol 24/7, reported that the company’s owner, Matt Mears, had emailed investors that their money would not be returned and the business would be winding down.

The closure follows two crowdfunding campaigns, first in 2017 and again in 2022.

"You put your money and trust into Temple, and I’m very sorry that the business hasn’t delivered the outcome we hoped for. I know this is disappointing news," Mears wrote, according to Bristol 24/7.

In the email, Mears explained the company had experienced issues with their supply chain along with rising costs for materials and energy, saying: "It’s an exceptionally difficult time to run a bicycle business."

"We’ve worked hard to turn the business around while managing persistent pressure on cash flow. We substantially reduced overheads, launched new products, relocated our headquarters and opened a new showroom.

"Our electric bike performed well, but this was offset by weaker sales elsewhere.

"The business also has existing debt commitments, and I don’t see a realistic route to generating the profits and cash reserves needed to meet them. Taken together, I no longer believe the current model offers a realistic route to a sustainable business," Mears said in his email.

Bristol 24/7 also reports that Mears hopes to continue in the bicycle industry, using his experience in another business focussed on parts and accessories.

Mears launched Temple in 2014 while still an engineering student at Bristol University, the business making a variety of steel-framed bikes, mostly using tubes from compatriot company, Birmingham-based Reynolds. Their range includes regular road bikes, gravel, hybrid and city bikes, alongside E-bikes and even step-through frames. As recently as April 2026, Temple opened a new workshop and retail on the outskirts of Bristol.

items.title: Even post-Mitchell Robinson, the Knicks are feasting on the glass
items.author: Michael Zeno
items.content:
When the Knicks lost Mitchell Robinson in the offseason, there was not only a sense of mourning for losing the services of the longest-tenured Knick right after a championship, but also in the sense of what he provided on the court.

Even with his injury-prone nature, Robinson was a premier rim protector and an anchor for the Knicks’ defense whenever he was on the court, which would be enough of an asset on his own, but the biggest asset he provided was something entirely different.

As we all came to know and love, he is simply the best offensive rebounder of this generation and one of the best rebounders, period, in the NBA. His innate ability to gobble up boards helped turbocharge an offense that already had plenty of offensive weapons, but would sometimes struggle with inefficiency.

For several years now, the Knicks have built their offense around the expectation of extra possessions. They’ve game-planned to win games by simply getting more opportunities to score than their opponents by grabbing more rebounds and committing fewer turnovers. With Robinson gone, the former was in serious danger, even if the team signed Andre Drummond to bandage it.

Through 10 games this season, though, they seem to have not missed a beat.

The Knicks are impressively the No. 1 rebounding team in basketball so far. That’s powered by Drummond not missing a beat with his usual rebounding prowess, but also an elevation in the team’s process and scheme.

Karl-Anthony Towns, historically a great rebounding center, leads the NBA with a staggering 13.8 rebounds per game. While his defensive strides have been the most encouraging part of the start of this season, he’s been a huge part of winning the possession battle by hitting another level with a 36.6 DREB%, which also leads the league.

As a team, the Knicks have hauled in 55.5 percent of available rebounds, 73 percent of defensive rebounds, and 38.8 percent of offensive rebounds, all leading the NBA. They’ve done this despite routinely having smaller lineups on the court.

Over the last two years, the Knicks were an elite rebounding team, especially thanks to double-big lineups and versatility. They’ve gradually gotten smaller as a team, have played zero minutes with more than one player taller than 6’8” on the court, and are still dominating on the glass.

Towns, Drummond, and Josh Hart have combined to do a bulk of the rebounding on both ends, but it’s also been a group effort. OG Anunoby has been much more active on the glass, averaging 1.7 OREB/g. Mikal Bridges and Jordan Clarkson are grabbing more rebounds on a rate basis. Even Jalen Brunson is averaging a career high in offensive rebounds.

Everyone is feeding off each other. Of the Knicks’ 10 most-used lineups, nine of them have an elite rebounding percentage, with the lone exception being a shocker: the starting five (47.5%).

Their early-season struggles, particularly on offense, are worth monitoring, but some positive regression is due whenever Hart returns from his ankle/illness ailments, especially in the rebounding department. The team as a whole played poorly through five games and has only started to pick it up recently.

The synergy has allowed them to just take the soul out of teams in recent games, something that’s been pivotal to their success in recent years. Just look at last night’s game against Milwaukee, where, despite the plucky Bucks chopping a 26-point lead down to 11, they couldn’t overcome a 59-32 rebounding disadvantage.

Against Cleveland on Saturday, the Knicks took advantage of no Jarrett Allen to outrebound the Cavs, 49-40, to help stretch their second-half cushion. In the blowout of the Bulls last week, it was another 57-34 bludgeoning.

It even makes you think: was it the system that made Mitchell Robinson who he was, or was he just a superpowered cog in the wheel?

Let’s slow down. Robinson was always a generational rebounder, as evidenced by his work under previous head coaches, but his early struggles in Boston are notable.

As long as Towns continues to be consistent defensively and the team keeps rebounding like this… will they even miss him that much?

items.title: 'If she has tears in her eyes, that is not a good sign' – Fears for Lucinda Brand's cyclo-cross season as world champion injures ankle in opening-lap crash
items.author: Owen Rogers
items.content:
Cyclo-cross World Champion Lucinda Brand season could be in doubt, after she was forced out of the Superprestige race at Niel in tears following an opening-lap crash that left her in tears.

Brand arrived for the Jaarmarktcross hoping to take her fifth win in the event, which formed the third round of the season-long Superprestige series, but the most innocuous of crashes left her barely able to walk.

She started the race on the back foot, trying to make up time on Amandine Fouquenet (Pauwels Sauzen-Altez Industriebouw), who had blazed her way through the sand pit to build an early lead. However, as Brand set off in pursuit in the muddy conditions, she was pushed into the barrier on a small climb, apparently twisting her ankle as her foot hit the ground.

While she carried on for a few seconds, riding through the pit area, she then abandoned and was barely able to stand as she dismounted. Though she was seen riding off, her Baloise-Poetsbureau team manager Sven Nys has cast doubt on the rest of her season.

"Lucinda twisted her ankle in the first round, where she made a misstep," Nys said in a statement from the team.

"She lost her line, she can’t put force on her foot right now, so I think it’s important that we monitor that and make sure that nothing was damaged. Hoping we won’t lose her for the rest of the season."

Nys also spoke with the host broadcaster Play Sports immediately after the race, saying: "She told me that she went off the track and wanted to put her foot down, but she twisted it, she couldn't put any weight on it anymore. I told her she needs to have everything checked to make sure no ligaments were damaged," Sporza reported him as saying.

"But if Lucinda has tears in her eyes, that is usually not a good sign. She is quite a tough cookie, which is why I am a bit worried now."

Brand has been the dominant force in cyclo-cross in recent seasons, winning the rainbow jersey twice, the World Cup and X2O Badkamers Trofee four times and the Superprestige on three occasions, as well as taking a total of 89 career wins.

At the weekend, she won her second European title after Luxembourgish rider Marie Schreiber was relegated for an irregular sprint.

items.title: Game Preview: Knicks vs. Cavaliers, November 11, 2026
items.author: Kento Kato
items.content:
Remember when the Knicks started 0-3, and people thought that the sky was falling? Turns out talks of the team no longer being good were exaggerated after all.

New York has now won six of their last seven games and are now winners of four straight after Tuesday night’s thrashing of a Bucks team that has been maybe even worse than expected. Part of that can and should be attributed to a lighter schedule over the last couple of weeks. The Knicks have played the 1-8 Bulls twice, the 2-8 Nets, and the aforementioned 1-10 Bucks. Of their two quality wins during that stretch, one was against the 7-3 Pistons and the other came against the Cavaliers, the latter perhaps not that great a deal given the interesting season they’ve had and the fact they were playing on the end of a back-to-back.

Up until the Bulls game last week, I would’ve called the Knicks’ season a roller coaster ride. But whatever early-season turbulence and disappointments the Knicks experienced, the Cavaliers might have surpassed it. At 5-6, they are just 1.5 games behind the Knicks. And it’s only been 11 games. But the Cavaliers have lost two in a row, have lost four of five and five of seven.

A lot of it starts with the starting lineup, which is ironic given the ceaseless talks surrounding the Knicks’ very own starters. Coming into Wednesday night, the Cavaliers’ preferred starting lineup of James Harden, Donovan Mitchell, Peyton Watson, Evan Mobley, and Jarrett Allen has an abysmal net rating of -18.9 in 84 minutes together. That number is a lot better when one of Mobley, Watson, or Allen is off the court, with the net ratings in those minutes all being positive, suggesting that the talent is there, but the synergy may not be.

There are three players in particular who deserve a closer look. Harden is currently averaging 15.3PPG and 5.7APG both of which are the third and fourth lowest of his career, respectively. He’s currently shooting just 35.5% from three, 37.5% from two, and shooting just 4.8FTA/G. Given how little he provides as a defender, he’s been a tough watch this season, and the numbers back it up. In the 359 minutes with Harden on the floor, the Cavaliers have had a -6.0 net rating. In the 174 minutes with him off the floor, they have a +16.5 net rating. That’s a 22.5-point swing.

He isn’t the only one that has been a disappointment, though. Watson, the Cavaliers’ major off-season trade acquisition, was looked to be the athletic shooting wing with size that could finally lock down the small forward position. Critics of the move were cautious given how much he benefitted from Nikola Jokic’s gravity and passing, but also given his relatively small sample size of being the kind of player the Cavaliers were hoping to get. While it’s unfair to judge Watson on just nine games in a new city and situation, he’s been a subpar player. Watson is currently averaging just 11.4PPG and 4.6RPG while having an assist-to-turnover ratio of 2.7:1.8 and is shooting a putrid 21.6% from three and barely hovering above 40% from the field. And like Harden, he’s been a negative when on the floor. The Cavaliers have a -5.2 net rating in the 250 minutes with him on the floor. Some of that may simply be due to the fact that he has to share a large chunk of his minutes with Harden. But it also doesn’t fully explain why the Cavaliers have a +7.1 net rating in the 283 minutes without him or why the starting lineup sans Watson actually has a +30.4 net rating in 23 minutes.

Maybe the most interesting case study, though, is Mobley. His individual stats look fine for the most part. He’s averaging 17.5PPG and 7.5RPG while shooting 55.8% from the field and 50% from three. But the Cavaliers are a -2.4 in his minutes. And even when he shares the floor with Mitchell and Allen, the trio is a -20.5 in 87 minutes. Meanwhile, the duo of Mitchell and Allen without Mobley is a whopping +26.1 in 67 minutes with Mitchell being a +7.0 in his minutes and Allen being a +5.0 in his.

The team can still turn things around. As Knicks fans were told to do after 144 regular season minutes, Cavaliers fans should be reminded to relax because it really is a marathon. But as you can see, there are some very clear holes in this team. Some have pointed to Kenny Atkinson’s inability to fully get this group to gel. I do think there is some validity to that. He’s either not making the requisite changes or his players aren’t listening. And either can be a fireable offense. But he can’t bear all of the blame.

The team has very little depth. And at the end of the day, it comes down to his players simply playing better. Harden can’t shoot this bad if he’s going to give close to zero effort defensively. Watson needs to shoot better. And Mobley, despite putting together a solid campaign statistically, needs to continue becoming much more of an aggressive force both offensively and defensively.

All that being said, the Knicks are in prime position to extend their winning streak to five. They took care of business against the lowly Bucks last night, which allowed their starters to rest. Not a single player played more than 29 minutes, so they should be ready tonight. It can be difficult to beat a team twice in such a short span, but given the Cavaliers’ recent struggles and how well the Knicks have played them as of late, New York should be favored.

When you play a team with expectations, such as the Cavaliers, that has underperformed the way they have, you run the risk of running into a hungry and sometimes even angry team. Cleveland has the talent on paper to beat anybody on any given night. But we saw last Saturday that this team doesn’t have a single player that can defend Jalen Brunson or Karl-Anthony Towns, and they just do not have the depth, especially at the center position, to reliably stay physical with a team like the Knicks.

With New York finally finding their groove and Cleveland slipping, I expect a closer game than the last one, but the Knicks to hold them off, improving to 7-4.

items.title: Hamilton loses 'most marketable athlete' status in 2026
items.author: Samarth Kanal
items.content:
Lewis Hamilton is no longer sport’s most marketable athlete - or even the most marketable Formula 1 driver, having fallen behind Ferrari team-mate Charles Leclerc - in the latest rankings created by media and events business SportsPro.

Hamilton was top of the 2025 SportsPro marketability rankings for athletes, with a total marketability score of 96.03 out of 100.

In 2026, Hamilton is ranked 22nd. His marketability score is 66.63, on par with footballers Neymar and Vinicius Junior.

Hamilton’s team-mate Leclerc is ahead in ninth on the list with a marketability score of 71.12, up from 25th in the 2025 list with a score of 75.03. 

The next-highest driver is Max Verstappen (48th, up from 81st last year), while 2025 champion Lando Norris (78th) is now ranked behind McLaren team-mate Oscar Piastri (56th) having been 23 places ahead in 41st last year.

New champion Kimi Antonelli is the lowest placed F1 driver who made the top 150 in 126th, a 48-place drop from 78th in 2025.

MotoGP rider Marc Marquez is the only motorsport athlete not tied to F1 on the list, ranking 86th, five places above Alpine F1 driver Pierre Gasly.

Belarusian tennis player Aryna Sabalenka is top of the list with, ahead of Chinese skier Eileen Gu, Greek basketball player Giannis Antetokounmpo, Norwegian footballer Erling Haaland, and Spanish tennis player Carlos Alcaraz.

American athletes make up 32% of the top 150 while British and Indian athletes are next with 7.3% of the pie apiece.

Football (soccer) has 33 athletes on the list and a 22% share of the list while motorsport’s eight representatives (5.3%) put it sixth on the list of sports, behind tennis and cricket but ahead of golf and boxing. 

Female NASCAR driver Toni Breidinger and F1 driver Liam Lawson dropped off the list having appeared in 2025.

How the marketability scores are calculated - why is Hamilton lower than Leclerc?

The marketability score is a combination of brand equity, momentum, and commercial trajectory, three metrics that are calculated by combining "several hundred data points" and more than 3000 brand partnership records over July 1, 2025, and June 30, 2026.

Scroll down to see how the motorsport athletes rank within the top 150.

Brand equity is the strength and trust of the athlete’s brand, momentum is the rate at which the athlete’s value is growing, and commercial trajectory is the room for an athlete’s future commercial growth. 

The latter metric is given the smallest weighting out of the three, and the scores are relative rather than absolute; Sabalenka’s ranking puts her top with the other athletes in mind. 

Leclerc, 29, has a higher brand equity score than Hamilton but a lower momentum score. The Monegasque’s ranking of commercial trajectory also boosts his ranking compared to Hamilton.

Age and longevity in the sport has an impact on the trajectory score: at 41 Hamilton is the joint-oldest athlete on the list with Cristiano Ronaldo and LeBron James.

Furthermore, Leclerc scores highly on the commercial trajectory metric, implying that there is strength in his brand that hasn’t been converted into commercial returns compared to Hamilton.

Leclerc scores high in brand equity due to his personal style and public presentation, plus the size of his audience and how actively that audience engages with his brand. 

Chris Collins, president of NorthStar (which powers the rankings) said to BlackBook Motorsport that Leclerc has "one of the strongest established brands of any athlete in the world.

"He ranks second of all 247 athletes we assessed on brand equity, built on how he presents himself, a compelling personal story and premium partners who keep choosing to work with him.

"As one of the most-followed drivers on the grid, it’s little surprise to see his audience scores performing well, but it also emphasises that his followers actively interact with his profile. He also benefits from a high audience breadth score, an expected outcome for all Formula 1 drivers thanks to their global profile."

He added of Hamilton: "What keeps him below the top 10 isn’t his brand, it’s time. At 41, there is naturally less career runway ahead, and a forward-looking assessment should read a great career in its later chapters exactly that way."

items.title: Superprestige Niel: Cameron Mason soloes to first win of the season and biggest victory of his career
items.author: cyclingnews@futurenet.com (Dani Ostanek)
items.content:
Cameron Mason (777TV) soloed to the biggest win of his career in the third round of the 2026-27 Superprestige, the Jaarmarktcross in Niel. The British champion got the better of Joran Wyseure (Crelan-Corendon) in a two-man battle over the final laps of the race.

The pair were the last men standing from a four-rider leading group after both Kevin Kuhn (Heizomat-Cube) and Michael Vanthourenhout (Pauwels Sauzen-Atlez Industriebouw) dropped away due to a puncture and a fall earlier on.

In the end, Mason carried a small gap into the closing eighth lap and pulled out a winning advantage in the sandpit before carrying a 20-second lead to the line to celebrate victory.

Joris Nieuwenhuis (Heizomat-Cube) grabbed the final podium spot, having been chasing the leaders alone since lap five. The Dutchman ended the race 27 seconds down on Mason and 12 seconds up on fourth-placed Felipe Orts (Euskaltel-Euskadi).

Mason now leads the Superprestige overall rankings, his 15-point haul taking him to 39 in three races, one better than Wyseure. Vanthourenhout is third overall on 37 points, having picked up just eight points here after finishing down in eighth place.

It was Kuhn who led from the start, with Vanthourenhout and Kuhn's teammate Nieuwenhuis getting separation from the rest to lead the chase. Further back, Wyseure and Niels Vendeputte were the best of the rest but over 10 seconds down.

Vanthourenhout left Nieuwenhuis behind on lap two to get across to Kuhn. Cameron Mason made it three up front on lap three, while Nieuwenhuis and Wyseure also came back as Kuhn continued to lead.

On lap four, Vanthourenhout took the lead, a second up on Kuhn, with the other three all within five seconds of him. Up front, the Belgian was beginning to pull away, however. Kuhn, Mason, and Nieuwenhuis dropped away, leaving Wyseure as the main chaser behind the leader, eight seconds back at the start of the fifth lap.

Vanthourenhout's spell out front wouldn't last long as Wyseure, Kuhn, and Mason all came back partway through the lap. The quartet were inseparable heading into lap six as Nieuwenhuis chased alone at 11 seconds down.

Kuhn, suffering a possible front puncture, was the first to drop from the lead group, losing contact with the front of the race and dropping back to Nieuwenhuis.

Wyseure took over the top spot heading into the latter part of the lap, though Vanthourenhout and Mason stuck with him into lap seven, the penultimate lap of the race. A Wyseure bike change to start the lap left him with a few seconds to make up, but he quickly came back to once again make it three up front.

Drama struck midway through the lap as Vanthourenhout fell while carrying his bike through a section of deep mud. He lost all momentum in pursuit of his fifth win of the season as a result, losing 20 seconds and dropping out of contention.

Up front, Mason and Wyseure continued in the lead with Nieuwenhuis chasing 10 seconds back. Mason had the advantage, though, leading the way and then pulling out a gap late in the lap to start the final lap four seconds up on Wyseure.

Mason's ability to ride through the sandpit made all the difference on the final lap, with Wyseure having to dismount in the chase. That meant Mason pulled out a 13-second gap and some breathing space heading into the latter part of the lap.

Mason kept pushing and made no mistakes through the mid-section of the lap, pulling out a 20-second gap to Wyseure, who was now only a handful of seconds up on Nieuwenhuis.

items.title: Who had the biggest breakout performances in the world of gravel in 2026? Here are six riders with top form through clouds of dust and mires of mud
items.author: jackie.tyson@futurenet.com (Jackie Tyson)
items.content:
The spotlight of gravel and mountain bike racing always shines on familiar performers like Keegan Swenson, Sofia Gomez Villafañe, Mads Würtz Schmidt, Kate Courtney and two-time gravel world champion Marianne Vos. They line up at an off-road race, and people pay attention.

However, deeper fields around the world now challenge these proven winners, coming from various backgrounds and fresh talent has made impressive moves to grab attention, especially at events in the UCI Gravel World Series, Gravel Earth Series and Life Time Grand Prix.

This year's UCI Gravel World Championships in Nannup, the first time in five years rainbow stripes were decided outside Europe, saw a gravel specialist win the men's race, Magnus Bak Klaris of Denmark. Of course, Vos reigns on all surfaces, but she was put to the test by Rosa Klöser, Larissa Hartog and Nele Laing, women who focus on dirt racing.

Because of the distance and cost to travel to Western Australia, as well as a conflict with Little Sugar MTB in Arkansas for many Life Time Grand Prix riders, some of the breakout rides happened long before races for rainbow stripes. The Traka continued to provide a platform for new stars, while Unbound Gravel always has storylines, during the mudfest itself and in the days following, like riders jumping into iconic US one-day races like Tulsa Tough or winning an unexpected US road title.

Who went from a supporting role to a leading role this season? Who was able to score a career-defining victory or podium?

Here is a collection of notable athletes we noticed from the 2026 calendar of off-road racing.

Magnus Bak Klaris certainly wasn't a rider off the gravel radar before 2026, with multiple Danish National Gravel Championships wins plus victories that included Santa Vall, The Rift and the UCI World Series race Wörthersee Gravel. However, at races like The Traka and Unbound, where the prestige and attention hit another level, Bak Klaris hadn't cut through to the podium step, plus his early-season results in 2026 weren't quite what they had been last season.

The 30-year-old rider, however, had certainly turned that around before 2026 was over. The signs of the building form were on display in September, when the previously missing season win tally started to build at Falling Leaves Lahti and then continued to roll on at Gravel Grit n' Grind. Still, even though he had finished in the top 10 at the UCI Gravel World Series in 2026, that was not enough to make him among the heavily marked men of the rainbow jersey race, which worked to his advantage.

"I didn't come in as one of the favourites, so I could maybe save some more energy than some of the others and hide a little bit," he told a small group of media, including following the event. That 'little bit' was enough to help propel him in the four-man sprint and claim a win that means he'll not be able to hide in the pack through 2027, not with the rainbow jersey on his back. (SG)

A one-time Zwift Academy finalist, Nele Laing entered the 2026 season with some promising gravel results after stepping into a few races in the UCI Gravel World Series and coming just off the podium at two of them. Though when she ventured over to the United States, now with the Canyon-DT Swiss squad, to try her hand at Sea Otter, she was definitely the wild card in the leading group of four that charged toward the line.

Impressive enough was her presence in Monterey alongside three-time US gravel champion Lauren Stephens (Aegis x Land of Enchantment), 2025 Traka 360 and Unbound 200 winner Karolina Migoń (PAS Racing) and the now four-time Life Time Grand Prix series winner Sofia Gomez Villafañe (Specialized Off-road). However, she wasn't just holding on but was the first of the four to put on the pressure through the crucial final section, and dropped Migoń as a result. Villafañe may have ultimately come over the top with Stephens following, but third at that early-season US race was more than enough to make sure she wouldn't be able to go unnoticed.

The 27-year-old then clearly showed that this was more than a one-off with third at The Traka, wins at UCI series events Hegau and 3Rides, plus a fourth at the UCI Gravel World Championships. Then, in a result that will help ensure she is keenly watched by rivals in 2027, she finished off the season by winning Nedbank Gravel Burn. (SG)

Victories define seasons for athletes, and one win stands out the most in 2026 for Bradyn Lange. Yes, he did win Sea Otter Classic Gravel in the stars-and-stripes jersey to take the top spot in the opening round of the Life Time Grand Prix. But it was how he won, out-sprinting four-time race winner Keegan Swenson with a crafty move on the final corner.

Lange proved his decision in 2025 to focus solely on gravel, or "try to be one of the best at one thing instead of good at multiple", was working. He won his first US national title in any discipline on the gravel roads of Minnesota. He moved to Canyon x DT Swiss ATR for the new year and won The Hills, a UCI Gravel World Series event in Italy, then finished second at The Traka 200 in Spain, and beat the best off-road rider in California.

The Oregon native still exhibited his mountain bike prowess with podiums at Leadville Trail 100 MTB and Chequamegon MTB, boosting him to his best finish in the Grand Prix across five years, finishing fifth on the elite men's leaderboard. He had the unique distinction of being the youngest rider in the Grand Prix field back in 2022 at age 21. Now at 27, he's got an early invitation to return for a sixth season, and he can no longer ride under the radar. (JT)

"A surreal experience" is how Kylee Hanel described making the main chase group at Big Sugar Gravel to finish fourth overall. While Stella Hobbs rode away with the solo victory, the 20-year-old held her own against the most dominant riders in off-road racing, Sofia Gomez Villafañe and Hayley Preen taking the final podium spots, while Hanel held off a charging Karolina Migoń.

She sealed the women's U23 title in the Life Time Grand Prix with top series points in all the races except Leadville Trail 100 MTB, where she finished second in the category. In between Sea Otter Gravel and the overall win at Unbound Gravel 100, she went back on the road with Aegis x LOE and went fourth overall at Tour of the Gila, with a stage win and youth classification title.

The multi-talented rider from Oregon competed for the first time at national events last year, where she had top 10s at US road and gravel nationals. Then this summer, she won the USPro U23 women's time trial national championship by 36 seconds over her closest competitor. She didn't realise at the time that it qualified her for Road Worlds, but knew it was a great opportunity for experience and to ride for Team USA in Montreal, even with two more Grand Prix races to follow in October.

"I'm the only one putting pressure on myself," she admitted to at the UCI Road World Championships, finishing 21st in the U23 time trial and 29th in the road race. The pressure was off when she landed on the wide-angle podium at Big Sugar. (JT)

Matthew Wilson may have been in the Life Time Grand Prix in 2025, but he walked away from last year with 'unfinished business' after not delivering the hoped-for results. With a new team in 2026, Scott Sports USA-Shimano, and determination to show what he was really capable of, Wilson went all out in pursuit of a wild card spot this year. The rider from New Zealand gained that spot, with 12th at Sea Otter Gravel and 28th at Unbound, but this time the best was yet to come.

Some indication of his early season form was already on display when the multi-discipline rider, who had come third at the New Zealand National Championships road race at the start of the year, washed off the mud of Kansas, borrowed a mate's road wheels and went straight to the top of a criterium podium at Tulsa Tough. Then, when he shifted into his mountain bike comfort zone at Leadville, his LifeTime journey all of a sudden took on a whole new complexion.

Wilson went from fighting for a start in the series to fighting for the top spots with his Leadville Trail 100 MTB runner-up spot and then a win at Chequamegon. Fifth at the season-ending Big Sugar Gravel was enough for a third-place overall and to clinch a guaranteed spot in 2026. There is now no doubting what the 25-year-old is truly capable of. (SG)

Martins Blums gained entry into this year's Life Time Grand Prix as a wild card with top finishes at Sea Otter Gravel and Unbound Gravel 200. A 12-time mountain champion of Latvia, including the 2024 Marathon MTB national title, Blums was in the chase group behind winner Matthew Wilsom at Chequamegon MTB and finished eighth. He then surprised the field in second overall at Big Sugar Gravel, where he surged from 12th to seventh overall in the final series standings.

Big Sugar was indeed big for his 31st birthday, racing with bib number 31. He made a breakaway group after backtracking from a wrong turn, finished on the podium in second place, and, with a series top-10 finish, earned his ticket to return in 2027.

He had limited gravel racing in his legs when he started at Sea Otter Gravel in California, but had support for his solo season from Scott Sport USA. Unbound was unfamiliar territory, which he said made him nervous, "but at the same time, it will be a cool challenge," he admitted on a social post. A knee injury at a World Cup mountain bike race in Switzerland kept him away from Leadville Trail 100 MTB, so we'll have to wait another year to see if his precision on a mountain bike can give Keegan Swenson a run for his money. (JT)

items.title: Superprestige Niel: Manon Bakker masters the mud to take the win
items.author: Owen Rogers
items.content:
Manon Bakker took her first Superrestige series win on Wednesday, the Velosport Veluwe rider dominating the race, riding alone to take the victory at the Jaarmarktcross in Niel.

Bakker escaped on the second of the five laps of the muddy course, eking out a lead and holding it. She eventually crossed the line 14 seconds ahead of Italian champion Sara Casasola (Crelan-Corendon) in second, with Denise Betsema (De Ceuster Bouwkranen) third.

The race was notable for the abandon of World Champion Lucinda Brand, the Baloise-Poetsbureau Lions rider crashing out on the opening lap.

With Bakker well ahead early on in the race, the day became a huge battle for the podium places, with Betsema edging clear first before Casasola launched her bid to close down Bakker late in the piece.

Bakker has had an excellent start to the year, opening her 2026/27 by winning six North American races from eight starts before returning to Europe for her first season riding as a privateer, running her own team.

In conditions which suited her to the ground, Bakker rode an almost flawless race, building her advantage quickly and defending brilliantly, slipping over only once, in the thick mud.

The third round of the season-long Superprestige series, the annual Jaarmarktcross in Niel, was held over five laps of a varied course, with plenty of sand, a series of what look like moguls, short sharp climbs, run-ups and plenty of mud.

The first sand pit came early in the lap, and, with none of the riders able to ride it, the bunch was spread in the first few hundred metres. Amandine Fouquenet (Pauwels Sauzen-Altez Industriebouw) exited in first place, and with teammate Leonie Bentveld behind her, the French rider quickly had a gap.

After winning the European title in controversial circumstances, Brand set off in pursuit. However, on one of the many short climbs she hit the barrier and was forced to retire from the race with an injury to her ankle.

As Brand rode back to her team camper, Fouquenet was caught, with Aniek van Alphen (777TV) and Bakker briefly gapping the two Pauwels Sauzen riders.

However, as the second lap wore on, the in-form Bakker, fresh from a clutch of race victories in North America, rode clear, taking a lead of 18 seconds into lap three ahead of an expanded six-woman chasing group.

At the end of the third lap, she had lost only one second of that advantage, with Betsema and Casasola beginning to eat away at the lead.

On the final lap, Casasola dropped Betsema and began to pressure Bakker, closing in, almost to within touching distance, but the Dutch rider held her nerve and form to take the win.

items.title: 'Increasing awareness between cyclists and motorists' – Garmin partners with navigation app Waze to increase rider safety with real-time alerts
items.author: Owen Rogers
items.content:
Bike tech company Garmin has announced a partnership with the user-based navigation app, Waze, to provide drivers using the app with real-time locations of riders.

It’s hoped the collaboration will increase rider safety, with drivers alerted to the presence of cyclists and better informed to slow down and take appropriate action. "By bringing Live Cycling Alerts to Waze, we’re giving drivers a helpful heads-up so they can slow down, stay aware and safely share the road," said Waze VP and GM, Gai Berkovich.

The system works when riders using one of Garmin’s compatible bike computers, like the new suite of Edge devices, or smartwatches activate the LiveTrack feature, using the Garmin Connect app on a smartphone. While this was created to allow riders the ability to share location, planned route and other features with family and friends, this now extends to the partnership with Waze.

"This collaboration brings greater peace of mind to cyclists by extending the benefit of LiveTrack to motorists using Waze for greater awareness of their surroundings," read the Garmin press release.

"Location sharing is temporary and session-based, and the cyclist’s personal information will not be shared or displayed in Waze." It also applies only to outdoor cycling activities.

Instead, what Waze users will see are 'Live Cycling Alerts' informing drivers of the cyclist’s presence on the road, with rider icons moving on the road in their vicinity.

"Garmin is well-known in the cycling industry for its safety-focused products and features, and we are excited to work with Waze to bring this unique feature to cyclists and drivers alike," said Garmin’s Vice President of Consumer Sales and Marketing, Susan Lyman.

"By increasing awareness between cyclists and motorists, this new tool is designed to foster a safer riding environment for Garmin customers by giving drivers valuable real-time visibility to their whereabouts, helping to create a more connected experience for everyone on the road."

Waze was created in 2009 as a community-based navigation application, which employs its users' generated travel information to provide the best navigation options.

What do you think? Will you activate this feature on your Garmin, can it really make your ride safer? Let us know in the comments.

items.title: What we know about worrying new Honda F1 reliability issue
items.author: Scott Mitchell-Malm
items.content:
Honda's worrying return of reliability problems includes a new issue, the root cause of which it might not trace before the end of the Formula 1 season.

Aston Martin and engine partner Honda suffered their third DNF of the triple-header in Brazil, when Lance Stroll retired for the second race in a row.

Stroll had two separate battery problems over the course of the Brazil weekend and didn't make it to mid-distance in Sunday's grand prix.

It means Stroll has finished just six of the 20 races held this season, while team-mate Fernando Alonso has had seven retirements of his own.

There have been some flashes of optimism - in relative terms, given how disastrous this first season of the new alliance has been - of late as Alonso scored points in Malaysia five races ago, had surprisingly good pace at Austin despite sustaining significant floor damage on the opening lap, and excelled in the wet in Brazil.

There, Alonso comfortably gave Aston Martin and Honda their best qualifying of the year, getting into Q3 for the first time and lining up eighth on the grid.

But this has been badly undercut by a return of significant fragility that's closer to how badly Honda started 2026.

Reliability problems also put paid to Alonso's chances in Mexico, where he had looked quite competitive and closer to the top 10 than normal. The issue was related to the cooling system inside the energy recovery system, whereas in Brazil the emergence of battery problems for Stroll sounded a clear alarm bell.

Shintaro Orihara, Honda's lead trackside engineer, acknowledged that "we know what happened, but we don't know what is the root cause".

He admitted it may take a few weeks to find that, but already from the data there needs to be some kind of countermeasure for the next race in Las Vegas, while Honda traces the underlying cause so it can be addressed properly for 2027.

"We need to find the actual root cause of this error for next year," he said.

"Otherwise, we keep having the same issue."

This was a different kind of failure to what had occurred in Mexico, which had led to MGU-K problems. But the theme is similar: in Mexico, Orihara had admitted to a lack of robustness within Honda's engine in more ways than one, and the fault there hadn't shown up in simulation.

Now Honda knows what happened but doesn't know why. That's a worrying through-line between the two issues. It also harks back to the start of the year, when Honda could identify the obvious catastrophic consequences of the problems that were emerging and could see broadly where they came from, but didn't know exactly what the problem's root was, because it had come out of the blue compared with what it had experienced on the dyno.

What's particularly alarming is that this does seem to be a regression from where Honda had got to in the middle of the season.

Its performance was obviously still lacking, and its engine is still underpowered on the internal combustion side, even with upgrades through the year to try to trim the deficit.

But it had at least got to a point where its cars were finishing races, which allowed Alonso to score some points when the Aston Martin was heavily upgraded.

Either side of the summer break, Alonso had five straight finishes, and Stroll got two of his six finishes this year in three races before the summer break too.

Orihara acknowledged that reliability was simply better in the middle of the season, but that has been replaced by "several issues" in recent races.

Some of this trend could be related to the mileage of parts - components simply coming to the end of their life cycle - or to just a case of Honda trying to run the engine harder for performance and going over the edge.

But with the battery issue that emerged in Brazil specifically, it's too early to say what the trigger was.

Honda has not made the progress it would have hoped for this season in terms of the all-round performance of the engine, and at best has only achieved some of its performance targets in very specific circumstances.

So the fact that reliability has got worse, without a clear upside, puts Honda under pressure and brings an unfortunate amount of negative scrutiny again, right at the end of a year in which it has had to come through quite a lot of adversity.

It is also a curveball for the development work Honda is doing on 2027, when it needs to take a step in both performance and reliability.

Everything that has been indicated so far is that there will not be a major step at the start of the new season. There's already a plan to phase in further upgrades through the year. But that work will already be deeply under way.

Troubleshooting takes away human resource, limited dyno hours which are restricted under F1's engine development limits, money that comes under the engine cost cap, and simply time because the clock is ticking to the start of 2027.

First the cooling issue in Mexico, whatever that was exactly, and now this on the battery side, takes Honda's focus away from a path that it would ideally be a lot further down.

Honda CEO Toshihiro Mibe was in Brazil, which Orihara said has a galvanising effect on the staff - "but on the other hand, we had a battery issue twice this weekend".

It was not exactly how Honda's F1 operation would have liked to present itself in front of the big boss. But, as Orihara noted, Mibe at least "knows what is happening trackside".

"He will bring this experience to the Japanese side and also boost our development," said Orihara.

If there was ever any possibility of complacency creeping in about how much work Honda has to do to reach the necessary standard, the CEO seeing first-hand the kind of problems still being encountered this deep into 2026 will have stamped it out.

items.title: 'I continued even after I thought it was fun' – Former U23 world champion retires aged 27
items.author: Patrick Fletcher
items.content:
Five years ago, Johan Price-Pejtersen looked to be on the verge of a highly successful career as a professional cyclist, but it is now fizzling out at the age of just 27.

The Danish rider claimed the U23 time trial world champion in Bruges in 2021, to go alongside his Danish and European titles. Beating Luke Plapp and Florian Vermeersch in Bruges, he announced himself as a future star and, though he did already have a professional contract with Uno-X, earned a move to the WorldTour with Bahrain Victorious.

After three years with that team, Price-Pejtesen spent the past two years with Alpecin-Premier Tech, but has decided to hang up his wheels at the end of 2026.

"It's an upheaval, but it's also a decision I made quite a long time ago," the 27-year-old said on the Danish Forhjulslir podcast.

"When you've been in cycling for a long time, you gain some experience. I've always said: 'I'll keep going until I don't think it's fun anymore'. Some things sound noble in the moment. The fact is that I continued riding my bike even after I thought it was fun."

As well as losing the passion for the sport, Price-Pejtersen also suggested he encountered physical problems that held him back.

"I had a period of two months where every time I went out to train, I felt like I had eaten something bad for breakfast, like I was going to throw up," he said.

"It's strange, but also true. I've spent some time thinking about it and getting used to it."

No pro win, controversially

Price-Pejtersen has raced sparingly since making his first and only Grand Tour appearance at this year's Giro d'Italia, where he placed a notable seventh in the time trial.

Since May he has only completed 10 race days, all on Danish soil, winding down his career with a final pro-level appearance at the Tour of Denmark followed by two criterium races.

Price-Pejtersen largely slotted into a domestique role over the years, and while he did achieve some strong results against the clock – including podiums at Tirreno-Adriatico and the Chrono des Nations – he never managed to win a race during his career.

items.title: 'We are certainly not doomed' – Thibau Nys and Lucinda Brand's cyclo-cross team in mid-season sponsor search after co-title sponsor pulls out
items.author: cyclingnews@futurenet.com (Dani Ostanek)
items.content:
Sven Nys' cyclo-cross team will be searching for a new title sponsor as Glowi, owner of cleaning agency Het Poetsbureau, is set to withdraw from its sponsorship deal at the end of this year.

Glowi took up a multi-year co-sponsorship of the team at the start of 2025, but the company had an option to withdraw at the end of each year.

"That option has now been exercised," Sven Nys, who runs the Baloise Verzekeringen-Het Poetsbureau Lions team, told Belgian newspaper .

The team currently have eight riders on their roster across the men's and women's elite and under-23 ranks, including recently-crowned European champions Thibau Nys and Lucinda Brand, and Annemarie Worst and Pim Ronhaar.

Thibau's father Sven said Glowi's decision to withdraw from sponsorship is unrelated to team results. reports that the company is facing its own difficulties.

"We built an incredibly good relationship with the people from Glowi and Het Poetsbureau, where I myself used to give cycling clinics to cleaning staff in all provinces. They were happy with our performance, and we gave them enormous visibility," Nys said.

"[The decision] is also completely unrelated to our team. They made a decision, and we respect it."

The team will continue with Baloise on board until the end of the 2027-28 cyclo-cross season, though they're now searching for a new co-title sponsor, with a contract set to begin mid-season.

"At a more difficult time for us than for a road team. Because we are in the middle of a cyclo-cross season and the contracts run until January 1. That leaves us in a tight spot," Nys said.

"In 2026, that applies to cycling in general and to every team looking for potential new partners. Unfortunately, in this sport, you are never all set.

"Companies that believe in us and 'want' to invest are our only income. It is a constant matter of keeping your feelers out. Discussions are ongoing. But you don't get something like this arranged in a few months."

Nys said that the team isn't in danger of disappearing from the cyclo-cross peloton this season.

He also denied that sports marketing and event company Golazo, which runs several cyclo-cross races and contributes to the team's youth structure and Sven Nys Academy, will step up to contribute to the senior squad.

"That is not true. We are part of 'the house', and they will of course continue to support us. But not in the way it is being suggested. No extra money will certainly need to be injected. In that respect, everything is covered for next year," he said.

"In the meantime, we have already found several additional shirt partners, who will be announced in the coming weeks. This means that we are already making concrete future plans.

"We are certainly not doomed. And we are diligently continuing our search... with the strong relationship with Golazo as a reliable foundation."
